title: Credit Score Prediction
projectType: Individual academic machine learning project
description: Developed and benchmarked multiclass credit-score classifiers on 25,000 initial customer-month records, comparing 8 model/feature-set combinations. The selected XGBoost model reached 0.6898 macro F1 and 70.79% accuracy on a 4,577-row group-disjoint evaluation set.
problemStatement: Predict customer credit-score categories (Good, Poor, and Standard) from financial behavior and credit history. Compare four machine learning algorithms and two feature-set strategies using customer-disjoint splitting and macro-averaged metrics.
businessContext: Credit scoring is a multiclass risk categorization task. This academic study explores how supervised learning may help analysts organize credit-risk patterns. It is not a validated lending decision system or a substitute for appropriate financial and fairness reviews.
dataset: Credit-score customer-month dataset (data_C.csv): 25,000 original observations and 29 columns including customer profile, credit facilities, loan details, repayment behavior, balances, and the Credit_Score target. After cleaning and filtering, the notebook reports 22,412 modeling records. Personal identifiers (Name, SSN, ID) are not model predictors.
datasetSize: 25,000 original records (29 columns) · 22,412 after cleaning · 17,835 train / 4,577 test · 3 classes
preprocessing: Audited missing values, inconsistent numeric/text formatting, duplicates and financial-value anomalies across 29 original columns.
Repaired inconsistent age and credit-related values, applied customer-based data consistency checks, and retained 22,412 records after documented cleaning.
Used StratifiedGroupKFold with Customer_ID as the group variable: 7,212 train customers and 1,830 test customers with zero overlapping customers.
Constructed sklearn Pipelines and ColumnTransformers: numerical median imputation, categorical most-frequent imputation and one-hot encoding; RobustScaler for the linear-model branch.
Excluded names, social security numbers and customer identifiers from the final classification features.
featureEngineering: Experiment A — Original + Feature Engineering (32 features): constructed EMI-, investment-, balance- and debt-to-salary ratios; credit-history missingness; nine loan-type flags; and spending/payment categories.
Experiment B — Original + Loan Flags (31 features): kept 17 numerical, 5 categorical and 9 binary loan-type features; this was the best-performing feature configuration.
Encoded loan categories such as mortgage, student, payday, auto, personal and debt-consolidation loans into model-ready binary flags.
methodology: Trained and tuned four algorithms — Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM — on both feature-set strategies (8 total trained/evaluated combinations).
For the engineered-feature comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 20 candidates and 5 stratified group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
For the original-plus-loan-flags comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 10 candidates and 3 group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
Used customer-disjoint train/test partitions (17,835 / 4,577 rows); tested all models with accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1 and multiclass one-vs-rest ROC-AUC.

Selected the final saved XGBoost configuration based on the notebook-reported test macro-F1 across the two feature sets; the associated final estimate should therefore be treated as exploratory rather than an independently confirmed holdout result.
results: Best recorded configuration: XGBoost with Original + Loan Flags (31 predictors); test macro F1 = 0.6898, accuracy = 70.79%, balanced accuracy = 0.7040, macro OvR ROC-AUC = 0.8591.
XGBoost using Original + Feature Engineering achieved macro F1 = 0.6860 and accuracy = 70.44%; both feature configurations outperformed Logistic Regression on macro F1.
Evaluated all 8 algorithm/feature-set combinations on the 4,577-row test partition; highest recorded macro F1 = 0.6898.
Verified zero Customer_ID overlap between train and test (7,212 vs. 1,830 customers); saved the selected pipeline and label encoder to a Joblib model artifact.
Best XGBoost confusion-matrix diagonal: 566 Good, 896 Poor, and 1,778 Standard predictions correctly classified.
insights: Using original numerical/categorical credit variables plus explicit loan-type flags slightly outperformed the more extensively engineered ratio-feature strategy on macro F1.
The dominant Standard class (13,282 of the original 25,000 records) makes macro-averaged metrics more informative than overall accuracy alone.
Group-based splitting is important because monthly observations may refer to the same customer; this split avoids customer overlap across train and test.
A comparison of class-level confusion matrices provides more context than accuracy alone, particularly for the Good and Poor categories.
businessImpact: Potential decision support for exploratory customer credit-risk segmentation and analyst-led case prioritization. Any regulated or production credit decision would require independent validation, calibration, explainability, bias/fairness checks, legal review and monitoring.
challenges: Correcting malformed numerical values and anomalous financial fields while preserving plausible credit-risk variation.
Handling repeated customer-month observations without customer overlap in evaluation.
Comparing linear and tree-based models under mixed numerical/categorical feature types and a nonuniform class distribution.
limitations: Reported metrics are sourced from the supplied notebook and have not been independently reproduced in this documentation.
The final algorithm/feature-set was chosen using test-set macro F1; a new untouched holdout or outer group-aware validation is needed for unbiased final model selection and evaluation.
Dataset cleaning occurred before the train/test split, so some preprocessing steps warrant an additional leakage audit and migration into a train-fitted pipeline.
The source dataset contains personally identifying fields and is intentionally not redistributed in the public GitHub package.
An end-to-end deployment of this specific credit-score artifact has not been confirmed from the four files supplied here.
futureImprovements: Introduce an independent final group holdout (or nested grouped cross-validation), keeping model selection away from final test data.
Place all learned data-cleaning statistics within train-fitted pipeline stages for leakage-safe reproducibility.
Add calibrated class probabilities, group-wise error analysis, model explainability, and fairness checks before any production-oriented use.
Document separate Streamlit / MLflow / AWS deployment evidence once the implementation files are provided.

title: Bank Marketing Campaign Classification
projectType: Group academic final project — Machine Learning (LA09, 4 contributors)
status: Completed group modeling experiment; notebook and poster verified
description: Collaborative classification study of 41,188 bank campaign records, comparing six models and class-imbalance strategies to prioritize likely term-deposit subscribers. Tuned Logistic Regression recorded 0.6979 cross-validated positive-class precision; held-out positive-class precision was approximately 0.67.
problemStatement: Predict whether a bank customer will subscribe to a term deposit (yes/no), with the modeling objective centered on precision for the positive (yes) class to support selective telemarketing outreach.
businessContext: The academic team examined how campaign response prediction could guide prospect prioritization and call-center resource allocation. The study reports exploratory metrics and does not claim a measured increase in real-world conversion or cost savings.
dataset: Bank Marketing — bank-additional-full.csv from the public Bank Marketing dataset linked in the original group notebook. The source has 41,188 rows and 21 variables: demographics, prior/current contact attributes, macroeconomic context, and binary response target y. The modeling notebook retained 40,184 rows and 20 columns after dropping default, removing duplicates, and filtering missing housing/loan fields.
datasetSize: 41,188 initial customer-contact records · 40,184 cleaned · 8,037 test observations · yes: 4,532 (11.28%) / no: 35,652 (88.72%) after cleaning
preprocessing: Converted categorical unknown markers to missing values; inspected six affected columns (job, marital, education, default, housing, loan).

Dropped the default feature following the group’s recorded chi-square investigation, removed 14 duplicated records, filled selected categorical unknown values as others, and removed observations missing housing or loan.
Encoded categorical features using one-hot encoding for selected fields and binary encoding for job, education, month and day_of_week through ColumnTransformer.
Created an 80/20 train–test split with random_state=100; the original notebook did not specify stratification for this split.
Excluded duration from the predictive feature set because call duration is not available before a telemarketing contact concludes.
featureEngineering: Constructed a categorical encoding pipeline combining OneHotEncoder and category_encoders.BinaryEncoder.
Compared training configurations without resampling, with RandomOverSampler and with RandomUnderSampler inside modeling pipelines.
Examined logistic regression coefficient magnitudes of transformed predictors; encoded month and contact features were prominent in the notebook output.
methodology: Conducted exploratory data analysis of target prevalence, employment-related macroeconomic attributes, previous contacts, job categories, marital status, education and communication channels.
Benchmarked Logistic Regression, KNN, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost and SVM with five-fold StratifiedKFold cross-validation, using positive-class precision as the benchmark score.
Compared baseline, random oversampling and random undersampling approaches within pipelines to assess the effect of imbalance handling on precision.
Selected Logistic Regression as the precision-oriented candidate, then ran RandomizedSearchCV with 100 parameter candidates × 5 CV folds (500 fits) on the training set.
Evaluated the tuned classifier on a held-out test set (8,037 rows) with per-class precision, recall, F1 and accuracy; inspected coefficients for encoded feature interpretation.
Preserved original group notebook output and figures; figures in this case study include original notebook plots and a chart derived directly from its recorded CV scores.
evaluationMetrics: Stratified 5-fold CV mean precision and standard deviation
results: Cleaned 41,188 original observations to 40,184 rows; target yes: 4,532 (11.28%), no: 35,652 (88.72%).
Six-model baseline five-fold CV precision ranking: Logistic Regression 0.6826, SVM 0.6391, XGBoost 0.5891, Random Forest 0.5507, KNN 0.5218, Decision Tree 0.3049 (from the notebook benchmark output).
Tuning Logistic Regression with RandomizedSearchCV increased mean cross-validated positive-class precision from 0.6826 to 0.6979 (+1.53 percentage points across the recorded experiments).
Tuned Logistic Regression test report: 8,037 samples (905 yes / 7,132 no); yes-class precision ≈ 0.67, recall ≈ 0.18, F1 ≈ 0.28, and overall accuracy ≈ 0.90.
Baseline comparisons included RandomOverSampler and RandomUnderSampler; neither resampled Logistic Regression configuration achieved the recorded no-resampling precision.
Original notebook visualizations analyze customer contact channels, jobs and demographic patterns; group poster documents the four collaborators.
insights: Precision is relevant for reducing unsuccessful outreach among predicted positives; however, at 0.18 recall the tuned model identifies only about 18% of actual subscribers, limiting campaign coverage.
The post-cleaning target is strongly imbalanced: about 11.28% yes, so 90% overall accuracy alone is not sufficient to judge value for finding subscribers.
Original EDA found higher observed conversion among certain contact channels and customer categories, but those associations are descriptive rather than evidence of causal uplift.
Call duration was analyzed for historical patterns but excluded from model inputs, consistent with trying to score customers before a call.
The group’s poster provides a shorter result summary; the more precise tuned CV metric (0.6979) comes from the final notebook output.
businessImpact: Academic prototype for ranking potential term-deposit prospects and discussing telemarketing efficiency. No production pilot, observed ROI, or realized bank conversion uplift is claimed.
challenges: Managing unknown categorical values, duplicate bank contacts and differing data types in the preprocessing pipeline.
Balancing outreach precision against low positive-class recall under substantial class imbalance.
Comparing resampling strategies and six classifiers before selecting a precision-oriented approach.
limitations: The result is group work by four students; individual technical contributions were not specified, so no exclusive ownership is claimed.
At the recorded operating threshold, test recall for the yes class is approximately 0.18 despite 0.67 precision: most true subscribers would not be identified.

Some cleaning and exploratory feature selection were conducted before the train–test split; the feature-selection step and preprocessing should be audited for potential leakage and reworked as train-fitted steps for production evaluation.
Several optimization runs in the notebook emit convergence warnings, and no reproducibility run has been performed in this packaging step.
No real campaign A/B test, production deployment, calibrated uplift model or realized telemarketing cost reduction was provided.
The group poster uses a different rounded CV precision snapshot from the final saved notebook; this case study uses the final notebook outputs.
futureImprovements: Tune decision thresholds according to business contact capacity and compare precision-recall curves, average precision and captured-positive volume.
Run nested or fully train-fitted preprocessing/feature selection with a stratified held-out test and reproducible random seeds.
Use cost-sensitive evaluation and outreach simulation to assess campaign value without asserting hypothetical savings as measured outcomes.
Add probability calibration and temporal validation against later bank marketing periods.

title: Bangladesh Crime Pattern Clustering — K-Means & PCA
projectType: Academic final project — Machine Learning
description: Explored 6,574 Bangladesh crime-related observations using data-quality assessment, mixed-type preprocessing, K-Means model selection, PCA visualization, and interpretable cluster profiling. Academic grade: A; historical experiment results are documented with reproducibility limitations.
problemStatement: Discover structurally similar groups among Bangladesh crime-related records without treating crime classification labels as a supervised target. Assess whether combinations of time, locality, weather, demographic, and infrastructure indicators form interpretable clusters and describe the boundaries of what such segmentation can establish.
businessContext: Crime-related data can be explored to compare observational patterns and prioritize further descriptive investigation. This coursework provides an exploratory segmentation workflow, not a validated crime-risk prediction system, causal explanation, geographic hotspot detector, or basis for operational policing decisions.
dataset: The original coursework identified Bangladesh_Crime_Dataset_B.csv with 6,574 rows and 26 source columns. Project discussions describe a mix of temporal, locality, precipitation/weather, demographic, institutional/infrastructure, and crime-related attributes. Specifically reviewed columns included part_of_the_day, season, precip, literacy_rate, religious_institution, and police_station; an Unnamed: 0 index-like column was considered for removal. The original dataset and notebook are no longer available for rerunning or independently checking the final training matrix.
datasetSize: 6,574 source observations × 26 columns (historical project inventory)
preprocessing: Inspected the initial 6,574-row, 26-column table, checking column types, missingness, duplicated rows, temporal ranges, category distributions, and out-of-range numeric values before clustering.

Documented missing observations for part_of_the_day (117), precip (657), season (328), and literacy_rate (328). Coursework notes describe mode imputation for categorical variables and median imputation for numerical variables; the exact final fitted preprocessing artifacts are unavailable.

Reviewed suspicious negative values in count-like infrastructure fields, including religious_institution and police_station, as invalid observations requiring cleaning rather than meaningful negative facility counts.
Checked duplicate records. Earlier project snapshots report conflicting duplicate counts (including 291 and zero), so no unverified final deduplication count or cleaned-row total is claimed.

Removed non-informative indexing or label-like fields from the unsupervised feature representation, as described in archived preprocessing notes; the exact final included-column list cannot be reconstructed without the notebook.

Applied categorical encoding and numerical scaling for distance-based K-Means. Archived notes reference OneHotEncoder for nominal categories, RobustScaler for numerics, and log1p transformation for skewed precipitation values.
Reviewed the final numeric feature representation before clustering and used PCA separately for exploratory two-dimensional visualization rather than as a substitute for cluster validation.
featureEngineering: Represented categorical context through one-hot indicators to avoid imposing an artificial numerical order on nominal categories.
Addressed differing numeric magnitudes through robust scaling so raw measurement units did not dominate Euclidean centroid distances.
Explored log1p(precip) to compress strongly right-skewed precipitation values while preserving zero precipitation, as described in the historical preprocessing discussion.
Kept cluster identifiers as derived analysis outputs, then compared groups using original contextual variables rather than interpreting cluster numbers as ordered severity levels.
methodology: Framed the task as unsupervised exploratory segmentation: patterns are learned from input feature similarity without a ground-truth cluster label.
Performed EDA and preprocessing to make mixed numeric/categorical contextual data suitable for a distance-based estimator; flagged data-quality caveats before interpreting group structure.
Fit K-Means candidates across multiple cluster counts (the archived tuning discussion references k=2 through k=10), and examined inertia/elbow behavior alongside silhouette and Davies–Bouldin scores.

Preferred a two-cluster K-Means solution in a documented tuning run because the reported silhouette was higher and Davies–Bouldin lower than for three clusters; lower inertia alone was not used to justify continually increasing k.
Used PCA to visualize the multidimensional data and examine apparent separation in a two-dimensional projection, recognizing that this projection may not preserve all original feature relationships.
Conducted cluster profiling to compare the contextual attributes represented by each segment; no verified final risk or crime-severity labels have been assigned to the groups.

Documented measurement uncertainty explicitly because the original source code, preprocessing pipeline, and exported experiment artifacts are no longer available to reproduce the reported tuning outcomes.
results: Original dataset inventory: 6,574 observations and 26 columns, combining crime-related and contextual variables. Final cleaned sample size cannot be established consistently from surviving notes.

Archived tuning table for one K-Means run: k=2 inertia 68,502.716, silhouette 0.842381, and Davies–Bouldin 0.173755. These are previously reported results, not metrics recalculated for this portfolio.
The same archived table reports k=3 silhouette 0.690448 and Davies–Bouldin 0.378465, supporting k=2 within that particular experiment.

A separate earlier discussion reported a best silhouette closer to 0.36. Since run-specific feature matrices, preprocessing settings, and saved notebook outputs are missing, this discrepancy cannot be resolved and the 0.842381 score should not be represented as an independently verified final benchmark.

An archived label-mapping step listed 5,644 and 864 clustered observations plus one unassigned row. These totals do not reconcile to the original 6,574 records; they are not treated as a definitive distribution for the complete dataset.
Project awarded academic Grade A. The notebook, datasets, raw visualizations, and reusable source code are unavailable; no public GitHub source repository or live application is claimed.
insights: In the documented two-versus-three-cluster comparison, higher silhouette and lower Davies–Bouldin for k=2 suggest stronger measured separation under the corresponding feature encoding and distance representation.

A high silhouette can also arise when a single feature or processing choice strongly partitions observations; cluster quality should be checked against feature distributions and domain interpretation before treating it as meaningful crime segmentation.

The original EDA identified nontrivial quality issues—missing weather/season/demographic values and invalid negative infrastructure counts—that can materially affect Euclidean clustering when left untreated.

Encoding strategy and robust scaling matter because K-Means minimizes squared Euclidean distances, which can overweight high-range numerics or unintentionally treat category IDs as ordered quantities.

PCA offers an interpretable visual summary but does not independently verify the real-world significance of two clusters; detailed profiles are needed before attaching substantive names or policy interpretations.

The recorded cluster membership appears uneven in an intermediate mapping, while missing rows and duplicate-check differences remain unresolved; these caveats prevent reliable statements about Bangladesh-wide prevalence or relative crime risk.
businessImpact: Academic and exploratory outcome: a repeatable analytical framework was studied for organizing contextual crime-related observations into groups, evaluating separation, and describing candidate segment characteristics. No causal inference, citywide crime-risk prediction, intervention outcome, or real-world adoption is claimed.
challenges: Preparing mixed numeric and categorical context for Euclidean distance clustering without artificial feature domination.
Handling missing precipitation, time-of-day, season, and literacy-rate entries while preserving interpretable feature profiles.
Recognizing impossible negative facility counts and inconsistent duplicate-count reports instead of silently treating every source value as valid.
Choosing a cluster count using multiple metrics and separating quantitative structure from unsupported real-world crime-risk narratives.
Reconstructing the analysis responsibly after loss of the original notebook and source dataset.
limitations: The original notebook and dataset were not recovered; historical metrics and decisions cannot be independently rerun or fully attributed to a single exact preprocessing configuration.
Different archived discussions record conflicting silhouette outcomes (approximately 0.36 and 0.842381); report the latter only as a specific archived experiment, not the validated definitive score.
Historical cluster-assignment counts do not reconcile to the raw dataset size. The final number of modeled rows, true duplicate removals, and individual cluster profiles remain unverified.
K-Means assumes similarity based on the transformed Euclidean feature space; arbitrary categories, skew, outliers, and feature weighting can change partitions substantially.
Principal-component visualization cannot establish causality, predict future crime, or validate that geographic or demographic group differences reflect true risk.
No original source-code repository, model artifact, deployed system, or authentic result chart is provided. The project is presented as an academic case study with Grade A.
futureImprovements: Recover or re-collect the exact licensed dataset and store a versioned feature dictionary, missingness report, and explicit duplicate-resolution log.
Reproduce preprocessing and K-Means in a single Pipeline/ColumnTransformer, record random seeds, feature weights, fitted transforms, and row-to-cluster identity mapping.
Compare cluster stability across seeds and feature subsets, evaluate alternative algorithms where appropriate, and profile the results using genuine original-scale variable distributions.
Re-run multiple-k evaluation and resolve conflicting historical scores and row counts before publishing an official experiment comparison figure.
Review demographic and geographic fairness implications before proposing any real-world decision-support use.

title: Content-Based Music Recommendation — TF-IDF & Cosine Similarity
projectType: Academic Machine Learning project
description: Developed an academic content-based song recommendation case study using a 4,999-track, 19-column music catalog. Explored audio and metadata quality, text-based TF-IDF feature representation, cosine-similarity ranking, and Top-N retrieval. Reconstructed documentation is grounded in historical discussions rather than recovered source code.
problemStatement: Provide relevant song suggestions from track attributes and metadata when user listening history, ratings, or collaborative-interaction data are unavailable. Explore how textual descriptions of track, artist, album, and genre can represent each catalog item for item-to-item similarity.
businessContext: Content-based retrieval can support catalog exploration, related-song discovery, and first-pass recommendations without needing collaborative behavior logs. Musical relevance is subjective; this coursework did not establish listening engagement, user satisfaction, or improvements to a deployed streaming product.
dataset: Archived coursework identifies song_recomendation_B.csv with 4,999 tracks and 19 fields. Metadata columns: Track URI, Track Name, Artist Name(s), Album Name, Album Release Date, Artist Genres, and Popularity. Twelve additional audio/music attributes: Danceability, Energy, Key, Loudness, Mode, Speechiness, Acousticness, Instrumentalness, Liveness, Valence, Tempo, and Time Signature. Reported data types: six object columns, twelve float64 columns, and one int64 column. The CSV itself is no longer available to recheck.
datasetSize: 4,999 tracks × 19 source columns (archived EDA)
preprocessing: Inspected the track catalog structure, metadata columns, audio-feature dtypes, missing values, and duplicated identifiers before selecting content fields for similarity analysis.

Archived df.info-style inspection records missing Artist Genres for 255 tracks (about 5.10%), Danceability for 252 (5.04%), and Instrumentalness for 102 (2.04%); several additional fields had only two missing entries. One separate historical note conflicts on the Album Release Date count, so no final total for that field is asserted.

Historical discussions recorded 13 exact-duplicate rows and 14 repeated Track URI values. A repeated URI is not automatically a safe record to discard; the exact deduplication result and final catalog size cannot be independently established.

Reviewed textual metadata for consistent missing-value handling and normalized string representation prior to content construction. Prior proposals included filling missing Artist Genres with 'unknown' and numeric audio features using a median, but the executed final imputation code is unavailable.

Reviewed valid ranges and outliers for acoustic/music attributes such as danceability, energy, instrumentalness, tempo, and loudness; archived guidance proposed range checks and clipping but did not preserve a final transformation report.
Kept the track identifier and display metadata distinct from vectorized model input fields, so similarity outputs can be mapped back to human-readable songs.

Avoided assuming album-release dates, popularity, or numerical audio features were all concatenated into the final TF-IDF representation. Original preprocessing artifacts and fitted transforms have not been recovered.
featureEngineering: Archived content-based design combines Track Name, Artist Name(s), Album Name, and Artist Genres into a text_soup profile for each candidate song.
A TF-IDF vectorizer represents distinctive word tokens in song profiles, reducing the influence of terms that appear throughout the catalog.

Proposed notebook settings included English stop-word removal, one- and two-word n-grams, and min_df=2; these parameters are documented as historical design guidance, not verified final model settings.

Audio fields including Danceability, Energy, Loudness, Acousticness, Instrumentalness, Valence and Tempo were inspected for richer music context. Whether they were combined into the exact final cosine-similarity matrix cannot be verified.

Maintained a track-to-row lookup concept for returning names, artists, albums, and genre metadata with ranked recommendations; exact matching and duplicate-title handling in the original code are not available.
methodology: Framed song recommendation as item-to-item content similarity rather than supervised classification or collaborative filtering based on user ratings.
Explored the composition and completeness of the 4,999-song dataset, with particular attention to missing genre information and danceability measures.
Prepared textual music metadata to form song-level content profiles, then used TF-IDF as the archived text-feature representation.
Used cosine similarity conceptually to rank tracks by the angle between nonzero TF-IDF feature vectors. Similarity measures metadata overlap, not actual listener preference or audio quality.

Historical example guidance described a Top-N retrieval function (default N=5) and genre/mood-style text queries such as 'dance pop pitbull party', 'classic rock rolling stones', and 'acoustic chill indie'. The code and resulting Top-N rankings were not preserved, so these are demonstration inputs rather than verified recommendation outputs.
Interpreted why metadata-rich and genre-consistent tracks would be easier for a TF-IDF retriever to match, while missing or generic artist-genre fields reduce the discriminatory signal.

Documented key differences between metadata similarity and numerical audio-feature similarity; the two should not be presented as one validated hybrid model without original feature concatenation code.
Summarized data quality, method design, limitations, and next-step evaluation in a source-code-free academic case study, without inventing similarity scores, selected songs, or deployment.
evaluationMetrics: Cosine similarity (ranking criterion, not a held-out relevance metric)
results: Historical project data inspection identified 4,999 music catalog rows across 19 columns, with six object, twelve float, and one integer type.

Reported missingness included Artist Genres: 255 / 4,999 (5.10%); Danceability: 252 / 4,999 (5.04%); Instrumentalness: 102 / 4,999 (2.04%). These figures are reconstructed from old project discussions, not recomputed from the CSV.
An archived duplicate inspection recorded 13 exact-duplicate rows and 14 repeated Track URI values. Cleaned observation counts are not available for verification.
Project notes and résumé summaries describe TF-IDF metadata-based recommendation with cosine-similarity Top-N ranking, while the exact final notebook and retrieved song lists are no longer available.
A Top-5 default and three text-query demonstrations were discussed in the archived notebook guidance, but no original ranked results or cosine-score outputs survived.
The academic project received Grade A as reported by the student. No trustworthy offline Precision@K, Recall@K, NDCG, coverage, or user-feedback experiment was recovered.
insights: The strongest documented data-quality gaps were in genre and danceability information. Missing Artist Genres can weaken genre-driven text retrieval because it removes valuable discriminating terms from the song profile.

TF-IDF rewards informative words that are uncommon across the song catalog, while cosine similarity emphasizes overlap in these weighted descriptors; it does not imply that the matched tracks actually sound alike.

A metadata-driven system can retrieve familiar artists, genres, and album-related content without observing user clicks or ratings, which is useful for item-level discovery but not personalized taste prediction.

Audio characteristics such as tempo, energy, acousticness, and valence describe musical properties differently from textual artist/genre identity. Combining these representations requires deliberate normalization and weighting, not just concatenating raw numbers into text.
Missing text descriptors, duplicate catalog records, generic genre tags, and repeated artist names can change recommendation diversity or produce overly homogeneous ranked lists.
A similarity ranking alone cannot establish recommendation quality; real evaluation requires relevance judgments, user feedback, benchmark labels, or credible proxy tasks.
businessImpact: Completed academic recommendation-system study (Grade A). Demonstrated the reasoning behind content-based catalog matching, metadata preprocessing, vectorization, and ranked retrieval. Commercial recommendation effectiveness, real user adoption, and deployment were not measured.
challenges: Handling substantial missing genre and danceability metadata while keeping track-level identity intact.
Detecting exact duplicate records versus repeated Track URI values without collapsing legitimately distinct catalog entries.
Representing song metadata with enough detail to distinguish meaningful matches while limiting noise from common text tokens.
Avoiding overclaiming metadata-overlap similarity as true acoustic or user-preference similarity.
Preserving academically accurate evidence after the original source notebook and output rankings were lost.
limitations: The original CSV, executed Jupyter notebook, fitted vectorizer, cosine-similarity matrix, and model output lists are unavailable; historical notes are the evidence for the documented workflow.
The exact TF-IDF hyperparameters, post-imputation catalog size, and any combined audio-plus-text scoring are not independently verified.
A separate historical note conflicts with the detailed df.info count for Album Release Date missingness; this case study does not invent a reconciled figure.
No recovered recommendation screenshots, true song ranking table, cosine output values, offline relevance metrics, user test, or deployed application exist in the available records.
Recommendations based on metadata can emphasize repeated artists and genres, underrepresent novel/diverse music, and reflect catalog completeness and tagging biases.
A Grade A course result indicates academic assessment, not proven production recommendation performance. No GitHub source-code repository is linked because authentic code is unavailable.
futureImprovements: Recover or obtain a properly licensed version of the same 4,999-track dataset, then rebuild a reproducible preprocessing and versioned data-quality report.
Recreate the documented TF-IDF content representation with explicit tokenization, missing-data policy, artist/genre weighting, and robust title/identifier matching.

Evaluate recommendation precision and diversity using annotated relevant-song sets, user ratings, or carefully defined proxy labels; report Precision@K, Recall@K, NDCG@K, coverage and novelty where meaningful.

Build an interactive search and explanation interface showing why a song was recommended and when the confidence in metadata matching is limited.

Benchmarked Logistic Regression, XGBoost and LightGBM on a held-out stratified validation set.
Tuned model hyperparameters using Optuna with 30 trials per algorithm and 5-fold cross-validation.
Logged baseline and optimized model runs in MLflow, including CV metrics and saved models.
Used XGBoost as the MLflow Model Registry @champion by optimized CV mean accuracy, while a separate notebook submission cell explicitly predicted using lr_final (Logistic Regression).
Documented Kaggle public leaderboard score separately from the notebook cross-validation experiment.
results: Kaggle screenshot: public score = 0.79401 for a successful submission; the screenshot does not establish which saved notebook revision generated the submission.
Original notebook baseline hold-out validation accuracy: LightGBM 0.81081, XGBoost 0.79931, Logistic Regression 0.76998.
