title: SPARC 2026 Finalist — Customer Repeat-Order Analytics
projectType: SPARC 2026 Data Science Competition — Finalist (3-member team)
description: SPARC 2026 finalist entry by a three-person team, centered on exploratory analysis and data preparation of 319,978 vehicle-sales transactions. Investigated duplicates, inconsistent customer records, demographic anomalies, geographic categories, product information and financing-data quality.
problemStatement: Explore historical vehicle sales and financing records to understand customer-transaction patterns and prepare trustworthy data for repeat-order analysis and customer follow-up prioritization.
businessContext: Competition: SPARC 2026. Team: Anang Tantowi, Hazel Novero Winata and Junico (team name: Trio Tunggal). The team reached the finalist stage. This public case study intentionally presents EDA and preprocessing work, rather than predictive-model scores, source code or purported commercial outcomes.
dataset: Historical vehicle-sales / financing transactions described in the team presentation: 319,978 initial transaction rows and 28 features spanning customer identifiers and demographics, motorbike products, dealers and geography, prices and financing details, payment methods, and dates. One row represents one transaction, not one unique customer; the EDA reports 266,927 distinct Customer_ID values.
datasetSize: 319,978 initial transactions · 28 features · 266,927 customer IDs (reported) · 317,637 rows after exact deduplication
preprocessing: Identified and removed 2,341 fully duplicated rows (319,978 → 317,637). Crucially, distinct transactions from the same customer were not treated as duplicate records because repeat activity is central to the study.
Validated customer identifiers against the documented CUST-XXXX format, excluding blank identifiers and aggregate TOTAL records that do not represent actual individual transactions.
Standardized payment-method codes (1 = cash; 2 = credit) and examined Finance Company values, including the special N category, before interpreting financing-related fields.

Audited malformed ages, with recorded values reaching 1,230 years. The presentation describes recomputing age from birth dates and retaining plausible ages from 17 to 90, rather than trusting unvalidated numeric age fields.

Assessed high-cardinality and inconsistent geographical fields. Removed Kelurahan, Kode POS and Wilayah from the selected feature set; retained Kecamatan after uppercase normalization, punctuation/space cleanup, and grouping categories with five or fewer records into OTHER.
Normalized dealer-area naming (including PPU = Penajam Paser Utara), treated numeric-looking dealer identifiers as categories, and reviewed the distribution of seven primary dealer regions.
Standardized vehicle-product categories such as Type Series, Segment, motorcycle model codes and colors; reviewed manufacturing-year values and filtered implausible years as described in the slides.
Converted heterogeneous money strings (such as Rp 2.056.000 and unformatted numbers) into numeric down-payment and installment fields; documented the derived fields dp_aktual_clean and cicilan_clean.

Compared cleaned down payments with On-the-Road (OTR) prices through dp_ratio = dp_aktual_clean / OTR. The slides report 65,103 credit transactions where down payment exceeded the vehicle price; these were flagged and excluded under the team’s documented business rule.
Reviewed tenor values and missingness. The presentation describes restricting selected financing records to tenors of 1–3 and identifying constant payment-method categories after filtering.
Rechecked residual missingness, notably Tgl Cetak and DLR Group at approximately 96% each in a later processing stage, before deciding which fields were usable for downstream analysis.

Reviewed statistical outliers in OTR, down payment and installment amounts using domain checks rather than indiscriminate deletion; the team presentation describes log transforming skewed price information.
featureEngineering: Geographical category normalization and rare-category consolidation for Kecamatan to reduce inconsistent labels and sparsity.
Numeric extraction of monetary values and a down-payment-to-vehicle-price ratio for transaction validation.
Categorical correction for dealer identifiers, motorbike product codes and sales-location labels.

Chronological customer-transaction grouping to distinguish one-time from repeat customers in a retrospective analysis; the presentation defines a repeat customer as one with more than one recorded transaction.
methodology: Data understanding: distinguished transaction records from unique customers, mapped the 28 original fields and checked sample distributions of age, payment method, vehicle price, dealership and product categories.
Numerical EDA: reviewed ranges, central tendency, right-skewed prices, zero values, age anomalies and unusual financial amounts requiring business validation.
Categorical EDA: explored customer identifiers, gender/other demographic attributes, geography, dealer regions, vehicle series, segment, color and credit-related categories.
Data quality audit: checked exact duplicates, invalid identifiers, inconsistent types and text, long-tailed geographic labels, hidden missing values, financing mismatches, and anomalous dates.

Preprocessing documentation: explained deduplication, normalization, targeted filtering, value-type conversion, category grouping, ratio checks and missingness reviews through original presentation slides.
Competition presentation: organized the findings and preprocessing decisions into a team case study that reached the finalist stage of SPARC 2026.
insights: The distinction between records and unique customers matters: 319,978 transactions correspond to a reported 266,927 distinct customer identifiers, so repeated customer IDs should not be dropped as if they were exact duplicate rows.
The data-quality audit identified 2,341 exact duplicate rows as well as more subtle anomalies involving age, customer identifiers, dates and monetary fields.

Geographic dimensions include numerous rare values and spelling variants. Retaining the most useful granularity while consolidating rare districts helps make descriptive segmentation more interpretable.
Vehicle prices were positively skewed; zeros and very high monetary values needed context-sensitive checks rather than automatic outlier removal.
The down-payment-to-OTR validation found concentrated inconsistencies in credit records, emphasizing the importance of testing business rules before interpreting financing patterns.
High missingness in some operational columns and imbalanced demographic categories called for cautious interpretation and further source-data checks.

A retrospective repeat-customer flag based on all recorded transactions describes historical repeat activity; prospective prediction would require a separate observation window and future outcome window to prevent temporal leakage.
businessImpact: Achieved finalist recognition at SPARC 2026 as part of a three-person team. The documented EDA and preprocessing work builds a clearer picture of transaction quality and customer behavior for a potential follow-up prioritization workflow; no quantified marketing uplift or predictive-model performance is claimed.
challenges: Distinguishing genuine repeated customer purchases from erroneous duplicate transaction rows.
Reconciling high-cardinality district labels and inconsistent formats across dealer and geographic attributes.
Handling implausible ages, nonstandard monetary strings, extensive missingness and inconsistent financing records without making unsupported assumptions.
Maintaining a meaningful customer-level analytical view from transaction-level records.
limitations: Numbers and cleaning rules in this case study are sourced from the team’s competition slide deck; the underlying customer-level dataset and code were not provided for an independent reproduction of the calculations.

The deck documents exclusion rules for unusual down-payment ratios and certain tenor values. These rules should be validated against the original data dictionary and finance-business definitions before reuse.
A full-history repeat flag is retrospective and would not by itself constitute leakage-free prospective repeat-order prediction.
No model training metrics, comparative prediction results, raw dataset or source-code repository are displayed, consistent with the scope selected for this public portfolio case study.
The source PDF also contains unrelated slides about Vision Transformers; only the relevant SPARC EDA/preprocessing slides are used here.
futureImprovements: Confirm disputed monetary and customer-identifier semantics with a formal data dictionary before applying irreversible filtering.
Document stage-by-stage row retention and field-level missingness alongside the existing cleaning decisions.
Validate temporal customer histories using a clearly specified historical observation period and a later repeat-order outcome period.
Monitor category consistency and data-quality rules across new monthly transaction batches.

title: InkluMap — Inclusive Learning Support Analytics Platform
projectType: End-to-end Data Science & Full-stack Web Application
description: Built an inclusive-school decision-support prototype that transforms 120 synthetic student assessments into interpretable accommodation groups, individual support recommendations, and school resource priorities. The system combines Python clustering experiments, a FastAPI/PostgreSQL backend, and a Next.js dashboard.
problemStatement: Schools supporting diverse learning needs must work with incomplete assessments, mixed numerical and categorical accommodations, and competing resource priorities. InkluMap organizes these inputs into interpretable needs profiles while preserving teacher oversight instead of treating clustering outputs as diagnoses.
businessContext: Designed as a local prototype for school administrators and educators: monitor assessment completion, explore five functional-needs groups, review student accommodations, flag high-priority cases, and plan resource allocation. The supplied records are synthetic demonstration data; real-school impact has not been established.
dataset: 120 synthetic student records were loaded from the project's CSV/Excel data source. 96 students with complete functional assessments were included in clustering, while the 18 incomplete and 6 not-started records remain visible in the management dashboard. The assessment includes eight ordinal need scores (0–3), material preferences, and assistive-tool categories.
datasetSize: 120 synthetic student records; 96 complete clustering cases; 18 encoded baseline features; 10 mixed-type Gower variables.
preprocessing: Imported and checked student assessment data from CSV/Excel sources, standardizing field names and student identifiers before modeling. The dashboard retains complete, incomplete, and not-started assessment states.
Filtered records to Status Asesmen = Lengkap for the clustering cohort (96 of 120 records); records without complete scores were not force-assigned to a cluster.
Validated student-code uniqueness, score ranges, and permitted material-preference and assistive-tool categories, and checked that the encoded clustering matrix contains no missing values.

Produced two aligned modeling representations: 18 encoded ordinal/binary features for the K-Means baseline and 10 original mixed-type variables for Gower distance (eight functional scores plus material preference and assistive tool).
Excluded existing output or intervention columns (cluster, dominant need, priority, recommendations, follow-up status) from model inputs to avoid circular cluster definitions and information leakage.
featureEngineering: Created eight functional-need indicators: visual access, hearing, communication, instruction comprehension, attention, mobility, assistance, and assessment adjustment; higher scores represent higher accommodation needs.
Encoded five learning-material preferences and five assistive-tool options as binary indicators for the 18-feature K-Means baseline.

Preserved material preference and assistive tool as categorical variables for Gower distance; scaled ordinal pairwise differences by observed feature range and calculated 0/1 mismatches for categories.

Generated cluster profiles and medoid-based representative cases; added rule-based priority, critical-access, unique-case, and teacher-review flags as downstream decision-support metadata rather than clustering input labels.
methodology: Established a K-Means baseline on the 18-feature encoded dataset, exploring multiple cluster counts and recording silhouette, Davies–Bouldin index, and inertia.
Computed a symmetric Gower dissimilarity matrix over 96 complete assessments using eight ordinal domains and two categorical attributes.

Evaluated Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering with precomputed Gower distance, comparing average and complete linkage across candidate cluster counts; selected five needs groups (average linkage, k=5) as the main interpretable segmentation.

Evaluated DBSCAN on Gower distances as a supporting unique-case detector; the best recorded candidate has silhouette 0.6869 but leaves four records classified as noise, so it is not substituted for the complete five-group segmentation.
Assigned a human-readable dominant need and group-level accommodation recommendations to each selected cluster using saved cluster catalog and risk-domain profiles.
Applied an explicit rule-based urgency framework to student profiles: high/medium/low priorities, critical-access review, and cases requiring educator verification.
Imported students, assessments, clustering outputs and recommended actions into a PostgreSQL-backed FastAPI service using SQLAlchemy models and Alembic migrations.
Built a responsive Next.js/TypeScript dashboard offering student records, assessment editing, group exploration, individual support suggestions, resource priority ranking, and print-to-PDF reports.
Documented local backend API tests, prototype usage, and installation. The repository is a functional local demonstration rather than a publicly hosted production instance.
models: Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering — Gower Distance + Average Linkage (selected)
evaluationMetrics: DBSCAN noise ratio and case review flags
results: Modeled 96 complete synthetic assessments from 120 total student records. 18 assessments were incomplete and six not yet started in the dashboard dataset.
K-Means baseline (k=5): silhouette 0.612864; Davies–Bouldin 0.563091, calculated in the encoded feature space.
Selected Hierarchical + Gower (average linkage, k=5): silhouette 0.675731 using precomputed mixed-type dissimilarities; cluster sizes were 20, 22, 18, 10, and 26.
Supporting DBSCAN candidate: silhouette 0.686897 with four noise cases (4.17% of 96); these outliers were flagged for review rather than replacing hierarchical segmentation.

Five functional-needs groups were described as structured instruction (20), visual access with auditory materials (22), hearing access and written communication (18), mobility/accessibility (10), and adaptive assessment with intensive support (26).
Rule-based priority summary of the 96 complete cases: 16 high, 73 medium, seven low; 40 critical-access review flags and 58 records flagged for human review. Flag counts may overlap.
Archived backend test output confirms 15 passed tests and one deprecation warning; the project README separately reports a 46-pass baseline, which has not been rerun as part of this portfolio review.
Local interface screenshots demonstrate student search and filters, individual functional score profiles, accommodation suggestions, and handling of incomplete assessments.
insights: Gower dissimilarity allowed ordinal support scores and categorical accommodation preferences to influence clustering without treating category codes as meaningful numeric distances.
Hierarchical clustering produced five complete, human-readable groups, whereas the DBSCAN experiment identified rare/unique cases that may benefit from separate educator attention.
The largest group (26 of 96) centers on adaptive evaluation and intensive assistance; identifying dominant needs helps translate statistical clusters into support-planning categories.
Incomplete assessments were not forced through the clustering workflow; the interface keeps them in the data-management flow for follow-up and completion.
School budget ranking is rule-based prioritization, not a predicted cost estimate, and teacher validation is explicitly part of individual decision-making.
businessImpact: Demonstrated an end-to-end approach for organizing accommodation assessments, surfacing group and individual support needs, and prioritizing review workload. The dashboard is a prototype based on synthetic data; improvements to student outcomes, costs, and real-school operations have not been measured.
challenges: Handling mixed ordinal and categorical data while keeping cluster profiles interpretable for non-technical educators.
Keeping incomplete assessments visible to staff without treating missing values as valid functional-need scores.
Translating unsupervised groups into explainable recommendations, priority rules, and manual verification instead of automated education decisions.
Maintaining consistent student identities across preprocessing, saved clustering outputs, PostgreSQL, FastAPI endpoints, and the Next.js frontend.
limitations: The dataset is synthetic and small (96 clustering cases), so the reported cluster separation does not establish real-world generalization or clinical validity.
Silhouette scores across K-Means, hierarchical Gower and DBSCAN are not a direct controlled comparison because their feature/distance representations differ.
The five groups reflect patterns in functional-need inputs; cluster membership cannot diagnose disability, infer student ability, or replace educator judgment.
Priority rules are configurable heuristics; resource-priority points are not currency amounts, and no cost-reduction benefit is claimed.
Live demo availability is not claimed: provided screenshots show the application running locally, and updating assessments does not automatically retrain clustering models.
futureImprovements: Validate the five needs profiles with special-education educators using larger, consented, representative datasets and review fairness/accessibility impacts.
Add authentication, role-based access, audit logs, encrypted sensitive storage, backup and production-safe deployment before real-student use.
Introduce versioned dataset snapshots and controlled retraining so school changes can be reviewed before regenerated cluster recommendations.
Conduct usability studies with teachers and accessibility testing; replace fixed urgency weights with validated school-specific planning criteria.

title: ASA DataFest 2026 Finalist — Patient Risk Journey Clustering
projectType: ASA DataFest BINUS 2026 · Team Bismillah · Competition finalist
description: Competition finalist case study focused on large-scale healthcare data integration and patient clustering: 7,675,801 original encounters, 9,313,853 merged records, and 57,386 patient profiles with 22 engineered features. Analyzed five social-risk and patient-journey segments, including a potentially under-screened high-risk group.
problemStatement: How can millions of encounters, diagnosis records and social-determinant responses be transformed into patient-level segments that reveal different care journeys and groups warranting closer screening? The portfolio case study focuses solely on the patient-clustering portion of the team presentation.
businessContext: ASA DataFest BINUS 2026, Team Bismillah. The submitted presentation interprets five exploratory patient segments by clinical/operational journey complexity and social determinants of health. This analysis is a nonclinical, descriptive segmentation study, not a validated diagnostic or triage system.
dataset: Seven linked healthcare source tables: encounters, patients, diagnosis, departments, providers, social_determinants, and TIGER census geographic codes. The saved notebook starts from 7,675,801 encounter records, then expands to 9,313,853 rows after sequential left joins. One-to-many diagnosis and social-response joins can increase row counts; the 9.31 million joined rows are not 9.31 million unique patients or independent visits.
datasetSize: 7,675,801 base encounters → 9,313,853 joined rows → 1,275,948 rows with social-determinant coverage → 1,210,243 clustering records → 57,386 distinct patient profiles × 22 features
preprocessing: Loaded seven source CSV tables into Pandas and made separate working copies: patients, encounters, diagnosis, departments, providers, social_determinants and tigercensuscodes.

Normalized the join keys as strings: trimmed whitespace, stripped accidental trailing .0 suffixes, replaced placeholder nulls with NaN and prepared CensusBlockGroupFipsCode/GEOID for geographic joining.

Verified foreign-key matching before joining. For example, patient join coverage was 7,353,621 of 7,675,801 encounter rows, while only 83,359 encounter keys initially matched a social-determinants record.

Performed sequential left joins: encounters + patients (7,675,801 rows), + diagnosis (8,099,023), + departments and providers, + TIGER geographic reference, + social determinants (9,313,853). Checked row counts and shapes at each step.
Audited nulls and repeated EncounterKey records after the social determinant join, then narrowed the merged table to 1,275,948 rows containing social-response information.
Removed rows with missing essential patient, disease-group and social-response fields, retaining 1,210,243 records for the clustering preparation.
Mapped DisplayName + AnswerText pairs to a custom ordinal social RiskScore (0/1/2 where applicable); maintained an is_missing indicator for noninterpretable or missing responses.
Filled 223,813 missing social RiskScore entries using their respective Domain mean values, keeping the originally missing-response flag for downstream analysis.
featureEngineering: Converted encounter/social-response rows to one patient per row using PatientDurableKey as the patient-level index.
Pivoted mean RiskScore into eleven domain features including stress, social connections, physical activity, food insecurity, housing stability, financial strain, transportation needs and depression.

Aggregated eleven patient-level risk and journey indicators: average/max/min/std social risk; question count and diversity; domain diversity; unique encounter count; unique disease-group count; missing rate; and missing count.
Joined domain scores and journey indicators into a 57,386 × 22 patient-feature matrix; missing engineered values were filled before StandardScaler transformation.
Used total_encounters and unique_diseases to visualize journey complexity, while composite social-risk scores described relative differences in screening responses.
methodology: Analyzed the clustering-only workflow from healthcare data integration to five interpretive patient groups, excluding the separate readmission and physician-shortage topics in the team presentation.
Standardized 22 heterogeneous patient features with StandardScaler before computing distances for K-Means.
Compared K-Means candidates k=2 through k=8 using inertia (elbow method) and sampled silhouette evaluation (up to 5,000 patient profiles).
The saved selection table records the highest silhouette coefficient at k=5 (0.327972) versus k=4 (0.325479), motivating the five-segment solution used in the final team slide.
Profiled groups by social-determinant domains, encounter counts, number of disease groups and disease-category distribution; used PCA as an exploratory two-dimensional clustering visualization.
Presented the final five-segment Patient Risk Journey Map, contrasting encounter visibility with relative social risk and annotated disease profiles, as shown in the team presentation.

Preserved the five cluster names and numbered labels exactly as presented: Cluster 1 Low Risk, Cluster 0 Moderate, Cluster 2 High Complexity, Cluster 3 Psychosocial High Risk, Cluster 4 Hidden High Risk.
evaluationMetrics: Cluster-level descriptive social-risk and journey profiles
results: Original encounter table: 7,675,801 rows. Sequential data integration produced 9,313,853 joined rows, including row growth caused by one-to-many joins.
Social-determinant screening filter retained 1,275,948 rows; required-field cleaning retained 1,210,243 clustering records.
Patient-level feature engineering produced 57,386 unique patient profiles represented by 22 clustering features.
K-Means candidate evaluation (k=2–8) recorded its highest sampled silhouette coefficient at k=5: 0.327972.
Final competition presentation described five segments: Low Risk (1), Moderate (0), High Complexity (2), Psychosocial High Risk (3), and Hidden High Risk (4).
The competition team reached the finalist stage, as reported by the project participant; the patient-clustering map was included in the final team presentation.
insights: Cluster 1 (Low Risk): comparatively low recorded social/clinical risk and a simple documented healthcare journey; mainly suggested for preventive-care discussion.
Cluster 0 (Moderate): average relative risk with many general check-ups; exploratory opportunity for early monitoring and lifestyle support.
Cluster 2 (High Complexity): frequent encounters and multiple disease groups, suggesting a more complex care journey and a potential need for coordinated follow-up.
Cluster 3 (Psychosocial High Risk): elevated stress and social/financial burdens with mental-health disease patterns; suggests an integrated clinical-and-social perspective.
Cluster 4 (Hidden High Risk): elevated derived social-risk signals despite low encounter visibility; a hypothesis for possible under-screening, not proof that every member is clinically high risk.
The presentation's central message is that encounter utilization alone does not establish patient risk; social determinants and screening coverage add useful descriptive context.
businessImpact: Translated a multi-million-row healthcare integration workflow into interpretable population-level segmentation for the ASA DataFest finalist presentation. The proposed use is to inform further screening, outreach planning and care-coordination research; patient-level clinical benefit or causal impact has not been demonstrated.
challenges: Managing joins across seven heterogeneous healthcare tables while monitoring one-to-many row amplification and inconsistent key representations.
Reducing millions of encounter and social-response rows to a consistent patient-level unit of analysis without mistaking join-expanded rows for independent patients.
Handling numerous sparse or uninterpretable social-survey answers and making the rule-based social-risk encoding auditable.
Comparing cluster count candidates efficiently for 57,386 rows with 22 features while keeping results interpretable to nontechnical stakeholders.
limitations: This is unsupervised exploratory segmentation. The custom social-risk mapping and mean imputation are heuristic, not clinically calibrated or externally validated risk scores.

The original clustering notebook contains a saved output showing only labels 0–3 even though the code specifies best_k=5; five labels and group descriptions are therefore grounded in the final presentation and prior project discussion, not treated as validated per-cluster counts from that cached cell.
Joining diagnosis and social-response tables increases row counts through one-to-many relationships; neither 9,313,853 joined rows nor 1,210,243 records represent unique patients.
Zero-filled missing domain aggregates and domain-mean risk imputations may affect cluster distances and interpretability.
Claims about hidden high risk, psychosocial burden and under-screening are descriptive screening hypotheses, not diagnoses, causal explanations or evidence of clinical outcomes.
Competition finalist status is reported by the project participant; the presentation supplied here does not itself include an official finalist confirmation.
futureImprovements: Rerun the final k=5 segmentation end-to-end and save a consistent five-cluster profile table, counts and labeled outputs for independent verification.
Audit and document one-to-many join cardinality and examine the sensitivity of cluster memberships to risk-score coding, imputation and domain coverage.
Test stability of patient segments across alternative time windows and evaluate them with domain experts before any clinical application.

title: Bank Marketing Subscription — Sequential vs Functional ANN
projectType: Deep Learning academic coursework
description: Compared two identically structured Keras ANN models built with Sequential and Functional APIs on the UCI Bank Marketing dataset (45,211 records). Conducted feature-level EDA, outlier-aware preprocessing, stratified 70:15:15 splitting, class-weighted training, and held-out test evaluation. Functional ANN achieved ROC-AUC 0.9189 and 85.50% positive-class recall, with the known post-call duration limitation.
problemStatement: Predict whether a banking customer subscribed to a term deposit after a direct marketing phone campaign (binary outcome y: yes/no), while studying equivalent ANN topologies defined with different Keras model-building APIs.
businessContext: The campaign-response dataset captures historical marketing interactions from a Portuguese bank. This is a retrospective customer-outcome classification exercise, not an operational pre-call lead-scoring system, because call duration is recorded after/during the contact.
dataset: Source: UCI Bank Marketing (Moro, Cortez & Rita), using bank-full.csv within bank.zip, loaded as a semicolon-separated file. The version used contains 45,211 rows, 16 predictor variables and target y (17 total columns). Attributes cover customer background, previous campaign history and current contact metadata. This is a different UCI Bank Marketing file from the 41,188-row bank-additional-full.csv used in the separate classical-ML marketing project.
datasetSize: 45,211 campaign records × 17 columns (16 inputs + binary target)
preprocessing: Loaded semicolon-delimited bank-full.csv and conducted dataset structure, numerical summary, categorical frequencies, boxplots, correlations, class imbalance and outlier EDA.

Identified all 45,211 rows as non-null at the Pandas dataframe level; categories such as 'unknown' may still represent unavailable information and were retained as their own categorical values rather than silently imputed.

Observed strongly right-skewed account balances (skewness approximately 8.36). The IQR outlier check highlighted 4,729 balance records outside the specified limits, but these were not automatically removed because large positive balances or overdrafts can be valid financial observations.
Recognized pdays=-1 as a domain-specific sentinel meaning no previous campaign contact, not a missing-data row to discard.

Retained numeric variables including age, balance, day, duration, campaign, pdays and previous. The saved implementation does not create additional engineered variables; the main transformation is scaling and one-hot encoding.
Performed stratified random splitting with seed 42: training 31,647 (70%), validation 6,782 (15%), test 6,782 (15%). The observed positive counts were 3,702 / 794 / 793 respectively.

Applied RobustScaler to seven numeric attributes to reduce scale sensitivity to skew and outliers, and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore') to nine categorical attributes. The resulting feature matrix had 51 columns.
Fitted ColumnTransformer only on training data and transformed validation and test with the fitted transformer; mapped target no=0 and yes=1.
Applied balanced class weights from training labels: negative weight approximately 0.5662, positive weight approximately 4.2743. This gives positive-class mistakes more influence during training.
featureEngineering: Encoded nominal job, marital, education, default, housing, loan, contact, month and previous-campaign-outcome categories without arbitrary ordinal rank.
Transformed numeric and categorical inputs to a 51-dimensional float32 representation for the ANN; no data-dependent transform was fit on the held-out sets.
Used train-derived class weights to handle the roughly 88.3% negative / 11.7% positive target imbalance.

Kept duration in the recorded experiment but explicitly identified it as a current-contact variable unavailable for prediction before the call; the notebook does not provide a duration-excluded comparison.
methodology: Defined binary deposit-subscription classification using UCI bank-full.csv (45,211 records) and examined demographic, account, loan, contact-duration and campaign-history features.
Constructed a leakage-aware preprocessing pipeline and stratified 70/15/15 train/validation/test split; class counts show substantial imbalance.
Built a Sequential ANN with dense ReLU layers of 128, 64 and 32 units, BatchNormalization, Dropout 0.30/0.25/0.20, L2 regularization, and sigmoid output.

Built a Functional API ANN with the same layer topology and training hyperparameters, so the study primarily compares implementation interfaces and stochastic training outcomes rather than different model families.
Compiled both models with Adam at learning rate 0.001, binary cross-entropy, and accuracy, ROC-AUC, precision and recall monitoring.
Trained with maximum 100 epochs, batch size 32, class weights, validation monitoring, EarlyStopping, ModelCheckpoint, CSVLogger and ReduceLROnPlateau.
Evaluated both models on the same untouched 6,782-row test split at a 0.5 positive prediction threshold, obtaining precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, classification report and confusion matrix.
Interpreted the recall-versus-precision trade-off in a minority class: high recall identifies most subscribers but the resulting positive predictions include many false positives.
Documented operational limitations: duration is unknown pre-call, and the random split does not assess out-of-time campaign generalization.
results: Data: 45,211 records and 17 original columns; 39,922 'no' (88.30%) and 5,289 'yes' (11.70%). Training/validation/test: 31,647 / 6,782 / 6,782 rows; encoded dimensionality 51.
Sequential ANN held-out test: accuracy 0.840755, precision 0.411035, recall 0.836066, F1 0.551122, ROC-AUC 0.915079 and Keras-reported test loss 0.348217.
Functional ANN held-out test: accuracy 0.838101, precision 0.408188, recall 0.854981, F1 0.552567, ROC-AUC 0.918852 and Keras-reported test loss 0.344654.
At the fixed 0.5 decision threshold, Functional ANN improved positive-class recall by approximately 1.89 percentage points with slightly lower precision and accuracy.
Both models have the same Dense/BatchNormalization/Dropout architecture. Marginal differences between one run of each cannot demonstrate inherent superiority of the Functional API.
The models were trained with duration available, which is recorded during or after an outreach call. The notebook does not establish accuracy for selecting prospects BEFORE contacting them.
All reported values were read directly from the uploaded executed notebook; the model was not retrained or checked against new data during this portfolio review.
insights: Deposit subscribers represent only 11.7% of this dataset, so accuracy alone can obscure poor positive-class identification. Recall, precision, F1 and ROC-AUC provide a clearer evaluation.

Class weighting penalizes false negatives on subscriptions more heavily, plausibly explaining recall above 83% but relatively low precision near 41%, with many predicted subscribers who did not actually subscribe.

The Functional model had marginally stronger positive recall and ROC-AUC, whereas Sequential had marginally stronger accuracy/precision. Because model structures match, this is an experimental outcome, not an intrinsic difference between APIs.
Bank balances are heavily right-skewed, making RobustScaler a reasonable choice for retaining legitimate extreme values instead of deleting them simply because of IQR flags.

The pdays=-1 sentinel represents absence of a past contact. Treating this as an ordinary interval value may conflate contact status with elapsed time, suggesting a future indicator-feature experiment.
Duration can provide strong information about successful past calls, but it makes a model unsuitable for pre-call outreach ranking unless duration is removed and performance is reevaluated.

The 45,211-row bank-full.csv experiment should not be conflated with the 41,188-row bank-additional-full.csv classic ML project; different source variants and pipelines produce incomparable raw scores.
businessImpact: Academic comparison of ANN implementation approaches for retrospective bank subscription outcomes with class-imbalance-aware evaluation and a 0.9189 ROC-AUC on the saved test split. No prospective customer outreach, confirmed financial lift, or production deployment was measured.
challenges: Diagnosing skewed numerical inputs and preserving plausible high/negative bank balances while avoiding distortion from feature scales.
Preserving stratification when subscription positives account for only about one in nine observations.
Ensuring numerical scaling and categorical encoding are fitted on training data only.
Balancing subscriber recall against false-positive follow-up costs when using strong positive-class weights.
Distinguishing a retrospective call-outcome classifier from a practical pre-call targeting model when call duration is a predictor.
limitations: Current-call duration is known only after/during telephone contact; including it makes the reported ROC-AUC and recall inapplicable to selecting customers before the call begins.
Dataset bank-full.csv is ordered by date according to UCI; random stratified splitting does not provide an out-of-time marketing validation.

Both ANN implementations share the same architecture and nearly identical training settings. The small reported differences may reflect random initialization, optimization variability or training-path stochasticity.
Positive precision is approximately 41%, requiring careful assessment of false-positive handling costs and probability threshold calibration.
The notebook uses 'unknown' as a valid categorical level and pdays=-1 as a numerical sentinel, both of which could benefit from additional domain-aware feature engineering.
No duration-free baseline, threshold-optimization experiment, multiple-seed confidence intervals, model deployment or financial outcome measurement is documented.
No public code repository is linked yet. The uploaded notebook is available to assemble an authentic repository if desired; course grade was not supplied.
futureImprovements: Build a second experiment excluding duration for realistic pre-call targeting, and report ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, precision/recall and calibration on an untouched chronological test period.
Benchmark against majority-class, logistic regression, tree ensembles and XGBoost using the same bank-full.csv splits, explicitly separating this dataset from the 41,188-row UCI alternative.
Test different classification thresholds and report business-cost curves for outbound call capacity, false alarms and missed subscribers.
Encode pdays=-1 as a 'never contacted' indicator and handle unknown contact-related categories explicitly; assess their contributions without post-outcome leakage.
Repeat each same-topology ANN experiment over multiple seeds and report variance rather than attributing stochastic differences to the Keras API.
Package the original notebook, dataset access instructions, requirements and verified outputs in a public source repository with UCI attribution.

title: Cherry Leaf Disease Classification — AlexNet vs EfficientNetB0
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning midterm project
description: Examined 3,642 cherry leaf images across five imbalanced classes; built a manual AlexNet baseline, tested three architectural modifications, and applied ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetB0 transfer learning. Reported 91.76% accuracy and 0.9185 weighted F1 on a shared validation/test subset, with the holdout limitation explicitly disclosed.
problemStatement: Classify five cherry-leaf visual conditions based on RGB image texture, color, lesions, scorching and perforations; evaluate whether architecture selection and transfer learning help on a small, imbalanced image catalog.
businessContext: The exercise explores image-based agricultural disease screening. The dataset is not an external field-validation benchmark, and reported predictions should not be used as autonomous crop diagnosis.
dataset: 3,642 RGB JPEG images grouped in five folders: Cherry_Leaf_Scorch (1,101), Cherry_purple_leaf_spot (987), Cherry_brown_spot (614), Cherry_Normal_leaf (500), and Cherry_shot_hole_disease (440). Original resolution observed as 800×1,000 pixels (aspect ratio 0.8). Source files are not included with the notebook upload.
datasetSize: 3,642 JPEG images · 5 classes
preprocessing: Counted images by class and inspected sample leaves; 1,101 Leaf Scorch images versus 440 Shot-hole Disease images showed meaningful class imbalance.

Inspected image dimensions and aspect ratio (800×1,000; width-to-height 0.8), checked for corrupted images (zero reported), and resized all inputs to 224×224×3. Square resizing changes the original aspect ratio and may distort geometry; constant input dimensions alone do not guarantee zero distortion.

Applied rescale=1/255 to the manual AlexNet data generators. Training augmentation included rotation up to 25°, width/height shifts 10%, zoom 20%, horizontal flipping, and brightness 0.8–1.2; these transforms were not applied to the evaluation subset.
Computed balanced class weights for the manual CNN experiments to reduce domination by majority classes; kept categorical/one-hot labels for five-class cross-entropy.

Used a separate EfficientNetB0 data pipeline with pixel inputs on their original 0–255 scale because the imported Keras application backbone includes internal input preprocessing. This was a necessary change relative to the earlier manually scaled generator.

Notebook's directory generators created 2,550 training images and 1,092 validation images with validation_split=0.3. The later 'test' generator reused subset='validation' on the same folders, so the requested independent 70:15:15 split was not implemented.
Used shuffle=False on the reported evaluation generator when aligning predicted probabilities with directory class labels for classification report, confusion matrix and AUC.
featureEngineering: Modeled visual features automatically using convolutional filters rather than handcrafted lesion descriptors.
Implemented a manual AlexNet-style sequence of 11×11, 5×5 and 3×3 convolutions followed by pooling and two large 4,096-unit dense layers.
Added BatchNormalization and progressively smaller dense heads in experimental modified CNNs, comparing stability and overfitting behavior.
Used an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetB0 frozen convolutional backbone with global average pooling, a Dense(256) layer, Dropout(0.2), and a five-neuron softmax head.
methodology: Established the five-category supervised classification problem and audited image distribution, class imbalance, representative class appearance and file integrity.

Trained a manually specified AlexNet baseline using Adam, categorical cross-entropy, and balanced class weights. The architecture contained 46,767,493 trainable parameters and showed stagnant training/validation accuracy around chance levels.
Tested three manual CNN modifications by adding BatchNormalization, reducing dense-layer size, lowering learning rates, and incorporating callbacks such as EarlyStopping and ReduceLROnPlateau.
Compared with a fourth modified approach using EfficientNetB0 with ImageNet weights and a frozen backbone. Model summary reported 4,378,792 total parameters, with 329,221 trainable.
Recorded learning curves, weighted precision/recall/F1, classification report, confusion matrix, and one-versus-rest class-wise ROC/AUC for the EfficientNet experiment.

Reported an EfficientNetB0 evaluation accuracy of 0.917582 and weighted F1 0.918513 on 1,092 validation-subset images. These figures are not held-out final test metrics because model selection and evaluation reused the same 30% images.

Interpreted the large transfer-learning improvement in light of pretrained features and reduced trainable parameter count, while noting that manual CNNs and EfficientNet were fed differently preprocessed input during the recorded model-comparison evaluation.
results: Dataset EDA: 3,642 images in five classes: 1,101 Leaf Scorch; 987 Purple Leaf Spot; 614 Brown Spot; 500 Normal Leaf; 440 Shot-hole Disease. Corrupted images reported: zero.
Manual AlexNet baseline had 46.77 million trainable parameters. Its recorded evaluation accuracy was 0.271062 and weighted F1 was 0.115612.

Final table reported the following accuracies: Modified Model 1, 0.244505; Model 2, 0.293040; Model 3, 0.120879; Model 4 (EfficientNetB0), 0.917582. This is not a strictly controlled cross-model ranking because the baseline/manual CNN input scaling differs from the EfficientNet evaluation generator.
EfficientNetB0 reported shared-subset accuracy 91.7582%, weighted precision 0.928558, weighted recall 0.917582, weighted F1 0.918513 and categorical cross-entropy loss 0.2909.
Reported multi-class ROC AUC (macro OvR) 0.9909 and weighted OvR AUC 0.9919, measured against the same shared validation/test subset.
Effective split in saved code: 2,550 train and 1,092 validation/test-shared images; despite a 70:15:15 task description, no independent 15% test set was separated.

All reported model metrics are existing notebook outputs, not independently retrained results. The source notebook and PDF are available as user-provided evidence, but no public GitHub source repository has yet been created.
insights: Class imbalance between Leaf Scorch and Shot-hole Disease motivated class weighting, and augmentation introduced reasonable image variations to make training less dependent on specific poses and lighting.

Manual AlexNet's two 4,096-unit dense layers created a high-parameter model that remained difficult to optimize on 3,642 images; the initial near-chance training curve suggests ineffective learning rather than proven classic overfitting.

EfficientNetB0 reused pretrained edge, texture and shape representations, needed fewer trained parameters, and required correct input scaling to work with its built-in preprocessing. These factors plausibly explain the much stronger reported validation performance.

Resizing 800×1,000 leaves directly to 224×224 changes aspect ratio from 0.8 to 1.0, potentially altering the shape of lesions and leaf contours; aspect-ratio-preserving resizing/padding would be a more controlled alternative.
The apparent large accuracy increase cannot be attributed to architecture alone: input preprocessing and training configurations changed, and there is no independent final test cohort.

A high ROC AUC on the reused holdout subset measures score separation under the current evaluation but is not proof of robust generalization to unseen farms, cameras, leaf species or disease prevalence.
businessImpact: Academic proof of concept for visual classification of five cherry-leaf conditions, with documented model comparisons and a reported 91.76% evaluation on a shared validation/test subset. No deployment, clinical/agricultural expert certification, or field-impact outcome is claimed.
challenges: Limited images relative to manual AlexNet's 46.8M trainable parameters and strong differences in class support.
Choosing augmentation and class weights without destroying leaf lesion patterns.
Diagnosing stalled training curves and selecting a lighter transferable visual representation.
Correcting scaling mismatch between generic ImageDataGenerator rescaling and EfficientNet application preprocessing.
Recognizing that validation and test reuse prevents reliable independent model generalization claims.
limitations: Evaluation design is 70% training + 30% shared validation/test, not the requested independent 70:15:15. The reported 91.76% is NOT an untouched final-test accuracy.

Manual CNN candidates were trained on rescaled 0–1 images, whereas the final comparison function passed the non-rescaled EfficientNet evaluation generator to all models. Their reported evaluation accuracies therefore cannot be treated as a fair head-to-head benchmark.
Trained model weights, original image dataset, external site holdout and production API are not included in the uploaded source files.
Square resize without padding distorts the original 800:1000 aspect ratio.
Potential overlap of visually related photographs across splits and effects of class imbalance were not separately audited for data leakage.
An academic grade and internal evaluation are not evidence of real-world diagnostic performance.
futureImprovements: Create a genuinely stratified and independent 70:15:15 train/validation/test split, storing immutable per-image manifests and checking exact/near duplicate images across partitions.
Apply evaluation preprocessing consistently for all models, and tune solely on validation data before reporting untouched test results.
Compare freezing versus partially unfreezing the EfficientNet backbone, report class-level F1 and calibration, and use domain-specific acquisition tests.
Preserve aspect ratio via padding/cropping with explicit visual checks; audit dataset leakage, lighting variation and disease-label quality.
Package source notebooks, reproducible requirements and clean dataset access instructions in a separate public repository after verifying permissions.

title: Used-Car Price Prediction — ANN Regression
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning midterm project
description: Built an ANN price-regression workflow from 2,000 used-car sales records, resolving mixed-format features and outliers, selecting 1,648 modeling cases, and comparing baseline versus modified Keras models. The modified model achieved test R² 0.8777 and RMSE 0.2625 on log-transformed prices.
problemStatement: Estimate a used vehicle's selling price from model, technical specifications, age, mileage, ownership, fuel type, transmission and location, while handling noisy mixed tabular inputs.
businessContext: Used-car price estimation can help dealerships perform consistency checks and comparative market analysis; the experiment does not provide production valuation guarantees or validated live-market pricing.
dataset: Source notebook loads 1B.parquet containing 2,000 vehicle sales and 18 initial columns. Relevant fields include name, year, selling_price (USD), km_driven, region/state/city, fuel, seller_type, transmission, owner, mileage, engine, max_power, torque and seats. Some values were invalid (year 3011, max_power -100), and two sale prices were missing. After the recorded cleaning/feature-engineering stages, 1,648 records entered the modeling split.
datasetSize: 2,000 source rows · 18 original columns · 1,648 modeled rows
preprocessing: Audited 2,000 × 18 data, including 2 missing selling_price targets, zero exact duplicate rows, mixed object/numeric fields, and right-skewed prices (mean about USD 6,501; median USD 4,500).
Checked out-of-domain values including year=3011 and max_power=-100. Examined potentially questionable km_driven values and high mileage rather than assuming every statistical outlier was wrong.
Parsed torque text with different units and RPM notation into torque_nm and torque_rpm numeric features. Converted object-formatted mileage to numeric input.
Reviewed categorical cardinality and location consistency; feature engineering combined age, usage intensity and technical ratios, while model features excluded record identifiers.
Transformed the strongly skewed selling_price target with log1p before fitting neural-network regression. Notebook's test MAE/RMSE/MSE are therefore in log-price units, not USD.
Final modeling matrix contained 1,648 records and 15 pre-encoding predictors; split randomly using SEED=42 into 1,153 training, 165 validation and 330 test observations (about 70:10:20).

Constructed state_high using mean training-set log price and a training-derived threshold, then removed State or Province as direct input. This prevents use of validation/test target values in the location encoding.

Used a train-fitted ColumnTransformer with StandardScaler on numeric features, OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore') on fuel, seller_type, transmission and brand, and ordinal mapping/passthrough for owner and state_high. Resulting ANN input dimension: 45.
Fitted numerical and categorical transformations on training data only, then transformed validation and test using the learned preprocessing objects.
featureEngineering: Derived brand information from the vehicle name and encoded nominal manufacturer/fuel/seller/transmission categories with One-Hot Encoding.
Extracted torque_nm and torque_rpm from mixed string values with different separators, casing and torque units.
Created vehicle age (car_age), usage intensity (km_per_year) and engine-to-power ratio (power_to_engine) to summarize depreciation and technical characteristics.
Explored skewness correction including log1p of selling_price and transformations of usage variables.
Constructed a training-target-derived binary state_high representation to summarize local price-level context without fitting it on held-out labels.
methodology: Performed column-by-column EDA with descriptive statistics, category frequencies, geographic consistency checks, missingness, outlier inspection, correlation plots, and right-skewness diagnostics.
Prepared model-ready data using tabular domain cleaning, feature engineering, log target, leakage-aware splits and train-only numerical/categorical transforms.
Created a Keras Sequential baseline ANN with two 90-unit ReLU hidden layers, BatchNormalization, Dropout(0.30), L2 weight regularization, a linear output, Adam optimizer and MSE loss.
Monitored training and validation learning curves with EarlyStopping, ReduceLROnPlateau, ModelCheckpoint and CSVLogger; reported train/validation/test MAE, MSE, RMSE and R².
Developed a modified ANN using a 90-unit then 45-unit ReLU architecture, BatchNormalization, lighter Dropout(0.10), linear output and Adam; compared using the existing split.
Measured the modified model on the held-out 330-row test set: MAE 0.207360, MSE 0.068883, RMSE 0.262455 and R² 0.877696, all on the logarithmic target except dimensionless R².
Compared baseline versus modified test RMSE and observed approximately 12.1% lower error in log-price scale. Used saved actual-vs-predicted and residual plots to examine remaining error.
Did not translate error into USD or claim percentage accuracy because no original-price inverse-transform evaluation is provided.
models: Modified feedforward ANN (90–45 ReLU + lower dropout)
results: Initial dataset: 2,000 rows and 18 original columns. Recorded final modeling cohort: 1,648 cases with 45 encoded/scaled input columns; training/validation/test splits: 1,153 / 165 / 330.
Price EDA: mean selling_price about USD 6,500.86, median USD 4,500; target skewness before log transform 4.4599. Two original rows had missing prices.
Baseline ANN held-out test: MAE 0.237316, RMSE 0.298535, MSE 0.089123, R² 0.841760, calculated on log1p(selling_price).
Modified ANN held-out test: MAE 0.207360, RMSE 0.262455, MSE 0.068883, R² 0.877696, calculated on log1p(selling_price).
Relative test RMSE improvement: approximately 12.1% over baseline in log-price space; this is not a claimed 12.1% reduction in dollar price error.
The fitted transforms were learned from train only. State-level target encoding was also derived only using training-set price labels before being applied to validation/test records.
The source notebook documents training curves and test residual charts. Raw parquet data and saved trained weights were not supplied; no independent recomputation or deployment is asserted.
insights: Missing target values, invalid production-year/power entries and mixed torque strings made domain-aware cleaning essential before any neural learning.
The mean selling price greatly exceeded median price because high-end examples extend the right tail; log1p compression reduced emphasis on extreme dollar magnitudes during MSE optimization.
Reducing hidden-layer size and dropout from the baseline lowered the measured held-out error, suggesting that a simpler regularization balance helped this particular dataset.
Train-only preprocessing and train-derived state_high avoid a common leakage mode where validation/test statistics influence fitted feature transformations.
With 1,648 modeling cases and 45 encoded inputs, interpretability and calibration remain practical challenges even when a neural model reaches R² near 0.878 on log prices.
Log-scale error cannot be read directly as price error in USD; to estimate dollar-level MAE or deployment utility, predictions must be inverse-transformed with expm1 before scoring.
businessImpact: Academic price-regression proof of concept using real-world-style vehicle attributes, with a documented improvement from R² 0.8418 to 0.8777 on held-out log-price targets. No deployment, realized pricing revenue or production dealership adoption is claimed.
challenges: Parsing mixed-format torque descriptions into consistent physical units and usable numeric columns.
Balancing outlier treatment with retention of genuine high-mileage and premium vehicles.
Handling high-cardinality geography and manufacturer fields without creating spurious ordinal relationships.
Preventing leakage when encoding locations with target-derived training statistics.
Interpreting test error measured on transformed prices rather than raw dollar amounts.
limitations: Original 1B.parquet source data and saved weights are not present in the uploaded notebook package, so raw data values and model outputs were not rerun independently.
All reported regression MAE/RMSE/MSE values are on log1p(selling_price), not USD. A separate inverse-transformed price evaluation was not recorded.
The reduction from 2,000 input records to 1,648 modeling rows reflects multiple cleaning steps, but a complete itemized removal ledger was not generated for the portfolio review.
Only two ANN configurations were compared; no traditional regression or tree-ensemble control model was documented for this particular final comparison.
Random split is suitable for this retrospective academic experiment but does not test temporal out-of-time pricing robustness.
Market conditions, regional price differences, unseen brands and possible target-encoding drift require additional evaluation before commercial usage.
futureImprovements: Recover the original source parquet dataset and record all filtering steps in a reproducible Pipeline with a versioned data dictionary.
Evaluate inverse-transformed USD MAE/RMSE/MAPE and compare against median-price, Ridge, Random Forest and gradient boosting baselines.
Cross-validate feature engineering and training-target encodings with out-of-fold training representations to reduce overfitting in-sample.
Test temporal and geographic holdouts, monitor drift, and validate across price bands, manufacturers and usage types.
Package source notebook, environment and model serialization in a reproducible repository after verifying data sharing permission.

title: AMD Closing-Price Forecasting — LSTM vs Naive Baseline
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning final project — time-series forecasting
description: Forecasted next trading-day AMD closing prices across 10,098 observations (1980–2020), using chronological validation, train-only scaling, and a 254-session holdout spanning early COVID-19 volatility. Compared baseline and tuned LSTMs with a naive last-price benchmark.
problemStatement: Can a tuned LSTM reliably predict the next AMD closing price when prices are non-stationary, highly autocorrelated, and exposed to abrupt market regime changes?
businessContext: A reproducible educational forecasting experiment: all test metrics are computed in original USD price units and compared against a last-observed-price benchmark; predictions are not trading recommendations.
dataset: AMD historical OHLCV price series; only Date and Close enter the model. Each observation is a trading day, not a calendar day.
datasetSize: 10,098 trading sessions, 1980-03-17 to 2020-04-01; 8,859 training, 985 validation, 254 test targets
preprocessing: Audited Date and Close: no nulls, duplicate dates, weekend rows, zero/negative Close or infinite closing prices.
Converted Date to datetime and sorted chronologically; preserved all genuine price shocks instead of deleting extreme returns.
Separated 2019-04-01 through 2020-04-01 (254 trading sessions) as the final out-of-sample test; split preceding data chronologically into 8,859 train and 985 validation rows.
Fit MinMaxScaler to training Close only. Out-of-range validation/test values were retained rather than refitting on later data.
Built next-trading-day sliding-window sequences with prior-period context at train/validation/test boundaries; no random shuffle.
Inverse-transformed prices before evaluating RMSE, MAE and MAPE.
featureEngineering: Used last five trading-day Close values for the required baseline (window=5, horizon=1).
Explored extended 20- and 60-session contexts for the modified model; selected the 60-session configuration on validation data.
Analyzed returns, rolling statistics and autocorrelation in EDA without leaking future indicators into input features.
methodology: Baseline model: LSTM(50, activation=ReLU) followed by Dense(1), trained with the required five-step input history.
Developed alternative LSTM settings and selected AMD W60 U32 No Dropout using validation RMSE; this candidate used a 60-day history, 32 LSTM units, tanh activation and Huber loss.
Benchmarked against naive forecasting, where the predicted Close is simply the previous trading day’s Close.
Evaluated the untouched final-year test on the same price scale after inversion; compared error metrics and price-trajectory plots.
results: Final test — naive last-close: RMSE 1.3745, MAE 0.9112, MAPE 2.4435%.
Final test — baseline LSTM: RMSE 3.2348, MAE 2.9075, MAPE 8.1176%.
Final test — modified AMD W60 U32 No Dropout: RMSE 1.8757, MAE 1.3268, MAPE 3.4720%.
Modified LSTM lowered RMSE by 42.01% versus baseline LSTM, but its RMSE remained approximately 36.47% higher than the naive forecast.
Test covers 2019-04-01 through 2020-04-01, including the early 2020 pandemic shock.
insights: Longer temporal context and a robust regression loss improved the weak five-day LSTM, but did not outperform the last-value benchmark.
Because closing-price levels are very persistent, copying the previous price is a stringent benchmark. A good-looking prediction curve is not sufficient evidence of predictive advantage.
Abrupt changes in AMD price and volatility create out-of-distribution periods that are difficult for a purely univariate model.
businessImpact: Demonstrates disciplined, leakage-aware time-series validation and honest comparison against a simple benchmark; no trading profitability or real-world deployment is claimed.
challenges: Strong price-level autocorrelation can exaggerate visual forecasting quality.
Price volatility and non-stationary market regimes challenge extrapolation into the 2020 stress period.
Test Close can exceed training price ranges; min–max scaling must not be refit on test data.
limitations: Modified LSTM still underperformed the naive last-price baseline on the final AMD test year.
Only lagged closing prices were modeled; exogenous macroeconomic or news factors were not used.
Historical results do not establish profitable trading performance or future-market accuracy.
futureImprovements: Evaluate multiple walk-forward periods, including volatility-regime stress tests.
Explore risk-adjusted directional metrics in addition to raw price-error metrics.

title: AAPL Closing-Price Forecasting — Relative-Log LSTM
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning final project — time-series forecasting
description: Forecasted next trading-day AAPL Close from 9,909 historical trading sessions using validation-selected LSTM configurations, train-only scaling and a 254-session 2019–2020 test. A relative-log 40-session LSTM slightly outperformed a naive last-close benchmark.
problemStatement: Can an LSTM predict next-day AAPL Close despite dramatic long-term price-level growth and test prices outside the training distribution?
businessContext: Univariate academic financial forecasting, not an investment or live trading product. Selection was based on chronological validation data and final results were compared with a simple last-price forecast.
dataset: AAPL historical stock prices; Date preserves the observed trading-session order and Close is the sole model input/target.
datasetSize: 9,909 trading sessions, 1980-12-12 to 2020-04-01; 8,689 training, 966 validation, 254 test targets
preprocessing: Validated chronological ordering, Date/Close completeness, duplicate dates, and genuine extreme observations.
Reserved 2019-04-01 through 2020-04-01 as a 254-trading-session final test; divided the earlier rows chronologically into 8,689 train and 966 validation observations.
Fit MinMaxScaler on training data only for price-level experiments and allowed scaled later periods to exceed the training range.
Built sequences using exclusively prior Close observations, including boundary context across chronological splits.
For relative-log experiments, predicted and reconstructed price changes with the last observed Close as anchor; evaluated all forecasts on the original USD price scale.
featureEngineering: Built five-observation windows for the prescribed one-session-ahead baseline.
Tested raw and transformed close-price representations and longer windows; best modified candidate used a 40-session window with a relative-log target.
EDA examined right-skew, stock-price distribution shift, rolling mean/standard deviation and price-versus-return autocorrelation.
methodology: Baseline: five-day input window, LSTM(50, ReLU), Dense(1).
Tuned candidate window/architecture and transformation choices using validation RMSE rather than test performance.
Selected AAPL Relative Log W40 U32 Huber: 40-session input context, LSTM 32 units, Huber loss, and last-close-anchored price reconstruction.
Used the same original-price RMSE, MAE and MAPE measures for naive last-close, baseline, and modified models on the final test year.
results: Final test — naive last-close: RMSE 6.2818, MAE 3.8313, MAPE 1.5693%.
Final test — baseline LSTM: RMSE 8.6425, MAE 7.3481, MAPE 3.0325%.
Final test — AAPL Relative Log W40 U32 Huber: RMSE 6.1952, MAE 3.8172, MAPE 1.5670%.
Modified model reduced RMSE by 28.32% versus the baseline LSTM and by a modest 1.38% versus the naive last-close forecast.
Validation-based model choice preceded final evaluation on the 254-session holdout with the early-2020 market shock.
insights: AAPL prices exhibited strong long-run upward drift; directly forecasting absolute prices was vulnerable to a severe chronological distribution shift.
Relative-log modeling around the last observed price better accommodates price-scale changes than an absolute-price target, though improvement over the naive forecast was small.
A high correlation between adjacent Close levels does not imply equally predictable returns or direction.
businessImpact: Illustrates transformation-aware time-series modeling, validation discipline and a fair last-price benchmark. No investment claims are made.
challenges: All 254 test prices exceeded the initial training-range maximum in the historical audit.
The final year includes sharp market declines that stress extrapolation.
limitations: Improvement over the naive test benchmark was marginal and observed on one holdout year.
Only univariate Close history was used; no fundamentals or market events were included.
Performance was not assessed as trading returns, fees or risk-adjusted outcomes.
futureImprovements: Use walk-forward re-evaluation over multiple market regimes.
Analyze robustness to different prediction horizons and volatility shocks.

title: Overhead-MNIST Autoencoder — 784-to-128 Image Compression
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning final project — unsupervised image reconstruction
description: Compressed 16,016 Parking Lot and Storage Tanks grayscale images from 784 pixels to 128 latent features. Compared a baseline convolutional autoencoder with nine tuned architectures, improving held-out reconstruction SSIM from 0.4864 to 0.7573 (+55.7% relative).
problemStatement: How much spatial structure can an autoencoder retain while compressing 28×28 grayscale overhead imagery from 784 pixel values to a 128-dimensional latent representation?
businessContext: An academic dimensionality-reduction and image-reconstruction experiment; class labels select the two image categories but are not reconstruction targets.
dataset: Overhead-MNIST v2 image and label files in IDX format. Combined original train/test images were filtered to Parking Lot (label 4) and Storage Tanks (label 9).
datasetSize: 16,016 selected 28×28 grayscale images: Parking Lot 8,007 and Storage Tanks 8,009; train 12,812, validation 1,602, test 1,602
preprocessing: Read IDX image/label binary headers and arrays; combined the provided original partitions before a required new split.
Selected labels 4 (Parking Lot) and 9 (Storage Tanks) from 76,777 original images; excluded all other classes.
Inspected class counts and pixel intensity distributions: Storage Tanks average intensity ≈155.38, Parking Lot ≈130.97 on a 0–255 scale.
Converted uint8 pixels to float32, scaled 0–255 into [0,1], and added a channel axis for (28,28,1) Conv2D input.
Used stratified train/validation/test splitting of 12,812 / 1,602 / 1,602 images (≈80/10/10) without fitting a train/test-dependent scaler.
Used each image as both the encoder input and decoder reconstruction target; labels were retained only for per-class evaluation.
featureEngineering: Baseline: Conv2D(16) → MaxPool2D → Flatten → Dense(128) bottleneck; decoder projects latent vector to feature maps and upsamples to 28×28.
Modified variants explored deeper convolutional encoder/decoder feature extraction while preserving the 128-dimensional bottleneck.
Compared model quality using reconstructed pixels and SSIM, including separate analyses for Parking Lot and Storage Tanks.
methodology: Trained baseline convolutional autoencoder with 128 latent features, batch size 64, learning rate 0.001 and up to 50 epochs.
Tuned nine modified architecture/hyperparameter configurations using validation SSIM; selection did not use the test split.
Selected Modified_AE_F48_F96_D256_LR0005_COMBINED: 48/96 convolutional filters, 256-unit dense layer, learning rate 0.0005, combined MSE+SSIM loss, batch size 64 and latent size 128.
Used EarlyStopping and ReduceLROnPlateau based on validation SSIM; measured held-out reconstruction SSIM, MSE and MAE after selecting the model.
Inspected original-versus-baseline-versus-modified image grids to explain the scores rather than relying only on a single aggregate metric.
results: Mean test SSIM improved from 0.48636776 (baseline) to 0.75727385 (modified): +0.2709061 absolute, +55.70% relative.
Modified best validation SSIM was 0.7542612; test standard deviation decreased from 0.201410 to 0.118133.
Parking Lot class-wise test SSIM improved from 0.363024 to 0.683231 (n=801 test samples).
Storage Tanks class-wise test SSIM improved from 0.609712 to 0.831317 (n=801 test samples).
Best modified test MSE was 0.014135923 and MAE was 0.08082049 on normalized pixels; bottleneck remained 128 dimensions.
insights: Storage Tanks reconstructed more reliably: brighter, more regular and often circular structures are easier to preserve than complex parking lines, cars, shadows and texture.
Combined MSE+SSIM loss rewards preservation of structural content, which helps explain the large SSIM improvement even though pixelwise MSE improved relatively little.
The 128-value representation compresses the 784-dimensional pixel vector, but reconstructed images still lose some fine details and should not be interpreted as lossless compression.
businessImpact: Demonstrates unsupervised representation learning, systematic validation-only model selection, and interpretable quantitative plus visual evaluation on grayscale overhead imagery.
challenges: Parking-lot textures contain thin high-frequency details that tend to blur with basic bottleneck reconstruction.
Combining structural and pixel losses requires checking generalization on an unseen test set.
limitations: SSIM measures similarity for input-to-output reconstruction, not classification accuracy or compression file size.
The two-class sample does not establish generalization to all satellite or aerial imagery.
Reconstruction is not lossless even after the improvement.
futureImprovements: Evaluate downstream utility of latent vectors for retrieval/clustering.
Compare a convolutional variational autoencoder while controlling latent dimension.

title: Overhead-MNIST — Conditional GAN vs Conditional DCGAN
projectType: Individual academic Deep Learning final project — conditional image generation
description: Generated class-conditioned 28×28 images of Parking Lots and Storage Tanks with a label-embedding CGAN and three Conditional DCGAN candidates. Best observed FID fell from 1159.40 to 1111.72 (4.11%), although outputs remained visually imperfect.
problemStatement: Can a label-conditioned generator learn separate image patterns for overhead Parking Lots and Storage Tanks rather than producing an uncontrolled mixture of classes?
businessContext: Educational conditional generative-modeling study; no claim of photorealistic generated imagery or production synthetic-data quality.
dataset: Overhead-MNIST IDX grayscale images; original labels 4 and 9 remapped to classes 0=Parking Lot and 1=Storage Tanks.
datasetSize: 14,232 two-class training images (7,111 Parking Lot + 7,121 Storage Tanks); 1,784 test images (896 + 888), 28×28 grayscale
preprocessing: Read original IDX train/test image and label files and filtered only Parking Lot (4) and Storage Tanks (9).
Remapped the selected labels to 0 and 1 to condition both generator and discriminator.
Converted pixel data to float32, normalized values from 0–255 into [-1,1] via (pixel - 127.5)/127.5, and reshaped to (28,28,1).
Chose tanh output for the generator so generated values share the same pixel scale as real images during adversarial training.
Converted/resized grayscale images consistently for InceptionV3 feature extraction in the FID evaluation pipeline.
featureEngineering: Added learned class-label embeddings concatenated with random noise at the generator input.
Conditioned discriminator decisions on both image and corresponding class-label embeddings.
Used 2048-dimensional InceptionV3 features to compare the real and synthetic image feature distributions.
methodology: Baseline: dense MLP Conditional GAN with generator Dense(128,256,512,1024) layers and discriminator Dense(512,1024,1024,512) layers; noise dimension 100.
Used a custom alternating training loop: update discriminator on real/fake images, then freeze discriminator for generator updates with fake-image targets set to real.
Trained the baseline with Adam (lr 0.00005; beta_1=0.5), batch size 128 and 100 epochs.
Replaced dense-only image processing with a Conditional DCGAN using Conv2DTranspose in the generator and convolutional feature extraction in the discriminator.

Explored three manual tuning configurations; best observed experiment used 128-D noise, batch 128, 100 steps/epoch, 150 epochs, generator LR 0.0002, discriminator LR 0.0001, 0.3 dropout and real-label smoothing 0.9.
Measured Fréchet Inception Distance using InceptionV3 features for 1,784 real test images and an equal number of generated samples. Candidate models were compared on this same test-reference FID.
results: Baseline MLP CGAN FID: 1159.4017.
Modified Conditional DCGAN experiments: FID 1141.6341, 1111.7247, and 1114.7536.
Best observed modified FID: 1111.724735 (Modified_DCGAN_Exp2_Noise128_BS128), a 4.11% decrease from baseline.
The best modified generator produced somewhat more structured samples, but recognizable class-specific geometry remained limited.
insights: Convolutional image generation can exploit spatial neighborhoods better than flattening every pixel into a dense network.
Although FID decreased, the absolute distance remained very large and generated samples still looked abstract; the experiment does not demonstrate realistic aerial-image synthesis.
An ImageNet-pretrained InceptionV3 encoder evaluates upsampled grayscale overhead imagery outside its natural-image training domain, so the absolute FID must be interpreted cautiously.
businessImpact: Demonstrates conditional generation, adversarial training loops, architecture iteration and metric-aware qualitative critique; the experiment is not presented as production-grade image generation.
challenges: GAN generator and discriminator training dynamics are sensitive to hyperparameters and relative learning speeds.
28×28 monochrome overhead images have limited spatial detail.
FID feature space may not match the aerial-image domain.
limitations: The three modified candidates were compared using FID against the test set; thus the reported best FID is a test-selected experimental result, not a completely independent final holdout estimate.
Absolute FID values exceeded 1000 and visual quality remained limited.
FID alone does not verify correct label conditioning, image diversity or absence of mode collapse.
futureImprovements: Use a validation subset for FID-based candidate selection, then reserve an independent test set.
Evaluate class-conditional precision, diversity and a domain-specific feature extractor; consider more stable GAN objectives.
