Applied z-score standardization to 7 measurements with detected IQR outliers, and min–max scaling to temp, pressure and free-flow travel time; checked raw-versus-scaled Pearson correlations.
Used Spark StringIndexer and OneHotEncoder for city, weather_main and weather_desc; stored OneHot vectors as strings for CSV persistence, while later modeling used indexed category columns.
Validated sensible ranges for humidity, wind speed, temperature, pressure, speeds, travel times and TomTom confidence; out-of-range measurements were converted to null.
featureEngineering: Created minute-resolution alignment key snapshot_min for two independently polled APIs; retained weather_snapshot_ts and traffic_snapshot_ts separately.
Built speed_ratio = current_speed / free_flow_speed (guarding against zero and missing denominator) as a normalized, segment-relative traffic indicator.
Defined descriptive rule-based labels from speed_ratio: Heavy <0.4, Medium 0.4–<0.8, Smooth ≥0.8. These labels are engineering thresholds, not independently measured ground-truth classes.
Created standardized and min–max scaled numerical variants and categorical encodings for subsequent exploratory modeling.
methodology: Source selection and spatial sampling: ten cities across Java and Sumatra, using one fixed latitude/longitude per city and TomTom Flow Segment Data for the road closest to that point.
API ingestion: two scheduled polling threads, JSON snapshot persistence and Spark Structured Streaming to micro-batch CSV outputs.
Temporal integration: join history data by minute bucket and matching city/coordinates; acknowledge that a minute bucket can create non-unique many-to-many matches.
Exploratory data quality checks: source schemas, numeric casting, IQR-based outlier counts, conditional scaling, categorical encoding and valid-range checks.
EDA: congestion-label frequencies, average speed ratio per sampled city location, time-series temperature snapshots, temperature-versus-speed-ratio scatter, and group-wise speed-ratio distributions.

Brief exploratory modeling only: the saved notebook performs a five-fold Spark CrossValidator fit for Logistic Regression, not an independent side-by-side benchmark of all three models described in the narrative.
models: Exploratory Logistic Regression (secondary; in-sample reported performance)
technologies: TomTom Traffic Flow Segment Data API
evaluationMetrics: Exploratory F1 / accuracy (in-sample; not independent validation)
results: Captured and processed two live API feeds across ten sampled Indonesian city coordinates. The joined, labeled dataset contains 740 rows; row counts may be inflated by minute-bucket many-to-many joining.

Rule-based congestion labels: Smooth 501/740 (67.70%), Medium 239/740 (32.30%), and Heavy 0. The absence of Heavy reflects this short sample and the defined speed-ratio threshold, not proof of no severe traffic in these cities.
Lowest average speed ratios at the sampled road segments: Yogyakarta 0.69398, Jakarta 0.75440 and Palembang 0.78346. These are not citywide traffic rankings.

Bandung, Semarang, Padang and Banda Aceh have observed mean speed ratios of 1.0 at their sampled segments, meaning the measured current speed closely matched free-flow speed during collected snapshots.

Outlier screening used ten numeric fields. Seven were standardized and three were min–max scaled; checking correlation before/after showed the expected preservation of Pearson relationships under positive linear scaling.

The notebook reports exploratory Logistic Regression F1 0.9676 and accuracy 0.9676, evaluated on the same dataset used in fitting/CV; this is an optimistic in-sample score, not a verified out-of-sample result.
insights: Traffic flow measurements are road-segment snapshots. A city sampled at one coordinate should never be used to claim its overall congestion ranking.

The abundance of Smooth and Medium labels is partly a consequence of the rule-based thresholds and the sampled minutes/segments; Heavy does not occur because none of the recorded speed ratios met its threshold.

High temperature–feels-like Pearson correlation (~0.957) is expected because both describe related atmospheric conditions; strong negative temperature–humidity correlation (~−0.899) is descriptive and may be confounded by geography, short collection times and repeated join rows.
Weak or visually inconsistent temperature–speed-ratio patterns do not establish that temperature causes traffic changes; road context, traffic demand and time-of-day were not controlled.
The 740-row join versus the nominal ~200 per feed is a data-quality lesson: align independent API feeds with key-uniqueness checks, closest-timestamp matching or aggregation before joining.
businessImpact: Demonstrates a practical prototype for combining external weather and road-traffic APIs into a Spark-based analytical pipeline. The notebook is an exploratory academic exercise and does not measure improvements in traffic management or deployment outcomes.
challenges: Synchronizing two independent API polling threads that return at slightly different timestamps.
Avoiding cardinality inflation when joining independent data feeds by coarse minute buckets.
Interpreting speed ratios from a single sampled road segment for each city.
Distinguishing source API signals from labels engineered out of the same traffic measurements.
limitations: Only a short capture period on 16 Dec 2025, with one fixed location sampled per city; findings do not generalize to full urban road networks, times of day or seasons.
No explicit proof of deduplicated one-to-one joins or independent temporal observations; 740 final rows may overrepresent repeated source snapshots.
The Heavy category is absent from the captured sample, making three-class model claims unsupported by this run.

The 0.9676 reported classification performance is computed on training data following cross-validation, without a held-out temporal test. It should not be used as a recruiter-facing performance claim.
Scaler and indexer were fit before cross-validation, and the congestion target was derived directly from traffic metrics, so leakage and optimistic validation risks remain.
The shared original notebook contains hard-coded API keys and must be sanitized before any public GitHub upload; keys should be rotated by the owner.
futureImprovements: Rotate exposed API keys, read credentials from protected environment variables and provide a public sanitized notebook.
Validate timestamp uniqueness and enforce one row per city per intended interval (or join by nearest time within a specified tolerance) before exploratory statistics.
Collect multiple monitored segments per city over longer periods with time-of-day and road-class features.
Profile missing responses, API HTTP failures, rate limits and confidence values; store request status and actual data timestamps separately.
Conduct an honest held-out chronological validation and avoid using target-derived columns and correlated target proxies as predictors.

title: Waste Material Image Classification — CNN & MobileNetV2 with Grad-CAM
projectType: Collaborative academic Deep Learning project
status: Completed team coursework — documented experimental results
description: Team computer-vision study classifying 2,527 images across six waste types. Compared baseline/improved CNNs against two fine-tuned MobileNetV2 variants; achieved a best recorded 81.32% test accuracy and inspected Grad-CAM attention maps. Describes class imbalance, per-class trade-offs, and test-based selection limitations.
problemStatement: Can a multiclass image-classification workflow recognize cardboard, glass, metal, paper, plastic and trash from product photos and reveal where its predictions focus visually?
businessContext: Automated sorting assistance could support exploratory recycling workflows, but this academic prototype has not been deployed at a sorting facility or validated on live recycling streams.
dataset: Dataset directory trash_images contained 2,527 labeled photos: paper 594, glass 501, plastic 482, metal 410, cardboard 403 and trash 137. Each image path's class folder defined the corresponding label. Original image assets are not published; preserved notebooks contain recorded samples and plots. No license to redistribute the underlying image collection was provided.
datasetSize: 2,527 waste images · 6 classes · 70:15:15 stratified split
preprocessing: Enumerated image paths and labels by class folder, built a Pandas dataframe, and mapped the six names to integer and one-hot labels.

Identified pronounced class imbalance: paper has 594 examples versus only 137 trash images (approximately 4.34 times as many). Checked examples for visually similar cardboard/paper, metal/glass and plastic/glass appearances.
Used stratified train_test_split with fixed seed 42 to create 1,768 train, 379 validation and 380 test images; the three sets are distinct in the recorded code.
Decoded all images to RGB and resized to 224×224×3, then normalized channels by dividing by 255. The notebooks do not establish a consistent native aspect ratio or pixel-level duplicate check.
Built TensorFlow tf.data pipelines with parallel image decoding, cache(), optional train-only shuffle(), batch(32), and prefetch(AUTOTUNE).

Applied training-only augmentation via horizontal flips, small rotations (0.05), zoom (0.05), translations (0.03), and contrast variation (0.08). Validation and test used the unaugmented image pipeline.
Calculated training-derived balanced class weights and manually adjusted glass weight to address low recall. The later MobileNetV2 V2 experiment also raised the trash-class weight.
For pretrained MobileNetV2 models, converted normalized [0,1] pixel data to [-1,1] using an internal Rescaling layer, consistent with the pretrained backbone's expected input range.
featureEngineering: Extracted image features automatically via convolution filters in the custom CNNs, then through ImageNet-pretrained representations in MobileNetV2.
Replaced Flatten with GlobalAveragePooling2D in the improved CNN to reduce parameter growth and emphasize per-channel global response.
Used class-weight tuning rather than oversampling to change training penalties for underrepresented or difficult categories.
Calculated Grad-CAM heatmaps from late convolution layers to examine attention for correctly and incorrectly classified images.
methodology: Started with EDA of 2,527 images, six class distributions, examples and dataset paths; standardized image dimensions and an identical stratified 70/15/15 partition.
Trained a baseline custom CNN with three convolution/pooling blocks (32, 64 and 128 filters), Flatten, Dense(128), Dropout(0.4), softmax and 10 training epochs.

Trained an improved custom CNN with four convolution blocks (32, 64, 128 and 256 filters), BatchNormalization, GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dense(256), Dropout(0.4), plus adjusted class weights and up to 30 epochs.
Developed MobileNetV2 V1 using ImageNet-pretrained weights, an initially frozen backbone followed by fine-tuning of selected top layers, and six-class classification head.
Tested MobileNetV2 V2 with altered dropout and class-weight emphasis, particularly on the underrepresented trash class; trained frozen and partially unfrozen phases.
Evaluated all variants on the same 380-image test set, recording Keras accuracy/precision/recall and separate sklearn per-class classification reports with macro and weighted F1.

Inspected original confusion matrices and Grad-CAM overlays. In the archived notebook, test metrics across candidate models were also used to identify the preferred variant; this can bias the selected test performance upward and should be corrected in future experiments.
Interpreted trade-offs across accuracy, recall and F1 rather than treating a marginal lead in aggregate accuracy as uniform superiority.
models: Improved CNN with BatchNormalization and GAP
evaluationMetrics: Macro / weighted F1 from classification reports
results: Dataset: 2,527 images. Stratified split: 1,768 training, 379 validation and 380 independent test images.
Baseline custom CNN: recorded test accuracy 0.547368, Keras precision 0.739362, Keras recall 0.365789, macro/weighted F1 approximately 0.55.

Improved CNN: recorded test accuracy 0.802632, Keras precision 0.871473, Keras recall 0.731579, macro/weighted F1 approximately 0.80. Baseline vs improved comparisons also reflect unequal training budgets.
MobileNetV2 V1: recorded test accuracy 0.813158, Keras precision 0.840456, Keras recall 0.776316, macro F1 approximately 0.78 and weighted F1 approximately 0.81.
MobileNetV2 V2: recorded test accuracy 0.797368, Keras precision 0.806630, Keras recall 0.768421, macro F1 approximately 0.78 and weighted F1 approximately 0.80.

Glass recall improved from 0.33 (baseline CNN) to 0.74 (improved CNN). The improvement co-occurred with architecture, regularization and weight changes, so the effect of custom class weights cannot be isolated.
Trash recall was 0.55 for MobileNetV2 V1 and 0.65 for V2. V2 improved this minority-class metric despite slightly weaker overall test accuracy.

Grad-CAM visualizations highlighted object regions in some correct predictions but also showed background sensitivity in misclassified examples. The method is interpretive, not proof of causal feature learning.
insights: The 594-versus-137 paper/trash imbalance can bias aggregate accuracy toward majority labels and makes rare-category recall important for practical sorting applications.
Visual similarities such as glass versus plastic or metal, and paper versus cardboard, are plausible sources of confusion because of shared shape, texture, translucency and reflective surfaces.

Improved CNN's additional normalization and GlobalAveragePooling were associated with much better performance than the 10-epoch baseline, but the models also had different training budgets, so it is not a controlled architectural ablation.

Transfer learning with ImageNet features and selective fine-tuning plausibly helped MobileNetV2 V1 identify general textures/shapes without learning all representations from scratch on only 2,527 images.
V1 achieved the highest recorded accuracy and weighted F1; V2 traded a small amount of aggregate accuracy for better trash recall, illustrating the need to select models based on actual error costs.
Original Keras precision and recall scores calculated directly on one-hot multiclass output do not equal macro-averaged per-class metrics; classification reports provide the latter.
Some incorrect predictions showed attention on backgrounds, illustrating that Grad-CAM visual plausibility alone is not a reliable deployment-readiness assessment.
businessImpact: Academic five-person team proof of concept covering preprocessing, multi-model CNN evaluation, transfer learning, and Grad-CAM. No observed financial savings, deployment, sorting-line test, or measured environmental outcomes were reported.
challenges: Strong target imbalance between common categories and the small trash class.
Distinct waste materials with visually similar colors, shine, texture and backgrounds.
Comparing handwritten CNNs against transfer learning with differing training compute and optimization setups.
Monitoring per-class performance instead of relying only on global classification accuracy.
Interpreting attention maps when models still attend to background artifacts.
limitations: Four architectures were examined with different training schedules, regularization and weighting configurations; performance differences cannot be causally attributed to a single technique.

The archived team selected the preferred candidate based partly on test outcomes, introducing possible model-selection bias. An ideal study selects hyperparameters using validation data and runs one untouched test evaluation.
No reported perceptual-hash check prevents near-duplicate images crossing random train/validation/test partitions, potentially affecting estimated generalization.
The dataset images and saved model checkpoints were not supplied, so experiments were not rerun for the portfolio review.
Grad-CAM may indicate regions influencing prediction but is not a complete causal explanation of visual decision-making.

Original team poster contains member names and student IDs; a cropped version without team identifiers is prepared for public sharing. The project is collaborative and no specific individual contributions are claimed.
No grade, live demo, operational recycling performance, or independently validated performance is asserted.
futureImprovements: Make an immutable 70:15:15 image manifest, detect exact/near duplicates and evaluate again on a genuinely untouched test cohort.
Select among model configurations using validation or nested evaluation, and compare identical training budgets before measuring generalization once.
Expand the rare trash class, diversify camera conditions, and assess out-of-domain objects and mixed-material waste.
Evaluate class-level precision/recall/F1 and confusion costs; tune decision thresholds or use cost-aware classification where appropriate.
Compare MobileNetV2 to EfficientNet and other efficient vision backbones under the same training protocol.
Check Grad-CAM robustness across many images and conduct simple segmentation/background-ablation tests.
